Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 90, to amend an Act relating to the establishment and expenses of the International Joint Commission under the Waterways Treaty of January 11, 1909.
He said:	This Bill is to make some
very minor changes in the Act. The Secretary of State for External Affairs is substituted for the Minister of Public Works, and some slight change is made in the clause relating to the expenses of the commission, 'but not in such a way as to increase the amounts already appropriated. The reason for the change is that proceedings before the International Joint Com-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: mission concern various departments from time to time, and occasionally more than one department, and it has been found not only convenient but necessary to detach a special officer for the purpose of watching these proceedings and safeguarding the interests of the country. For that reason Mr. Stewart, chief of the Hydrographic Survey was selected. He was appointed by Order in Council, as a temporary measure, to devote his whole time to the consideration of these cases, and he has been very fully occupied. In the United States they have a better system for that purpose than we have. All these matters are dealt with by a board of military engineers; they go to the War Department as a matter of course. We have not any corresponding organization which is so readily available; but we hope to find some more effective means of seeing that the interests of the country are properly safeguarded in these proceedings, some of which are of great importance in many respects. Some have so affected the interests of the provinces that they have been represented by counsel before the commissioners.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do I understand that the principal object of the Bill is to place the work under the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To have the Department of External Affairs take charge, as it were, of all these applications, so that it can communicate with the various departments and see that they are attending to the matter. Sometimes, when more than one department is concerned, that seems to be absolutely necessary; otherwise there is a lack of co-ordination of effort.
When is the Pecuniary Claims Commission to sit in Washington?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My colleague the Postmaster General tells me that it will sit almost at once-that the British Commissioner is leaving to-morrow for Washington.

Does the department contemplate increasing the salaries of the light-keepers in the near future?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A great many representations have been made to the department during the last year urging that there should be an increase in the salaries of the lightkeepers, but I understand that a general increase in the salaries of the lightkeepers took place within the last few years. While the department will give consideration to these representations, I would inform my hon. friend that the item under consideration does not provide for any general increase. The salaries are fixed on a certain scale, the lightkeepers

of a certain class are all paid the same and those of other classes receive the same salary.
How many lightkeepers participated in that increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It was a general increase; every lighthouse keeper in the service participated in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been n; change in that respect within the years that I have been in the department.
I understand that lighthouse keepers are obliged to provide their own coal at the lighthouses?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

There are some places where it is very difficult to get coal. Vessels charge a very high rate of freight to land coal at islands and places where there aTe no landing wharfs. Are lighthouse keepers obliged to pay these excessive freight rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
There are places where
there are difficulties in getting coal and in those cases the department furnishes the coal to the lighthouse keeper and charges him the actual cost.

That is actual cost of the
coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes. There are some
cases where it is impossible to get anyone to deliver the coal and then it is done by one of the Government vessels at actual cost.
There are no freight charges?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The lightkeeper is charged the actual cost of the coal without adding the cost of transporting the coal in a Government vessel to the lighthouse.

Is any distinction drawn between lightkeepers who are able to obtain wood for fuel and those who are living on islands or in places where there is no wood? I frequently have complaints that certain lighthouse keepers are in a position to supply themselves with fuel at
very little cost while others have to pay a very large amount for coal delivered by Government steamer or in some other way. Has the minister looked into that question?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am told there is no difference made in the salaries of the lighthouse keepers in consequence of the conditions that are suggested by my hon. friend.
I would suggest .that the minister look into that and ask his inspector to report on cases of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Of course, my hon. friend knows that the classification of the different stations depends to some extent upon whether they are situated a short distance from civilization or the base of supplies. That is all taken into account in fixing the salaries of the different classes and by that means the department believe that th y equalize things pretty well.

I would like to a,sk the minister if he has given instructions to the keeper of the Yarmouth light not to act as a pilot for vessels coming to the port of Yarmouth. It has been the custom for the lightkeeper at that station to do the piloting; in fact, about all the pilotage for vessels coming into the port has been d me by the lightkeeper. I understand the department have given notice to Mr. Doane, the lightkeeper, that in future he must notact as pilot. Is that the case?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter was brought up in the department in regard to the lighthouse keeper at the station to wh ch my hon. friend (Mr. Law) referred acting as pilot, it was discussed by the offic'als and their opinion was that a man must not absent himself from his light and that if a gentleman was acting as pilot he would have to be away from his light for a c n-siderable period of time. I am not prepared to say whether actual instructions were issued to him or not that he must not under any circumstances act as pilot, but I have no doubt that his attention was called to the fact that his duties as lighthouse - keeper required his constant attendance at his light and that it would he improper to engage in any other pursuits which would take him away from his light for any length of time.

There is a lightkeeper and an assistant and the light has never been left without somebody in charge of it. I know that the present lightkeeper has been acting as pilot in Yarmouth for a great

many years, or ever since he has been the lightkeeper, and that he is one of the best pilots at that port. I would like to ask the minister where the complaints came from.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not recollect at present.

If the minister knows that
these complaints came in I should think he would know w'here they came from.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not remember.
Who is acting as pilot now in Yarmouth harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know.
It is somewhat singular that the minister would give instructions to the lightkeeper not to act as pilot and not know whether there are any other pilots there or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think the hon.
gentleman would expect me to remember the names of all the pilots in all the different ports,

The hon. gentleman remembers a great many things that he would not be expected to know while there are other things in reference to his department that he appears not to remember. If the port of Yarmouth is left without a pilot it is a very serious matter, and Mr. Doane being one of the best pilots there, it seems a hardship that he is debarred from exercising a privilege which he has enjoyed for a great many years.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
I would like to know if the minister has any information to give -to the committee regarding the statement made in the papers a month or six weeks [DOT]ago, at the time of the unfortunate wreck of the Cobequid, that the lights were out of order and that the entrance to the bay of Fundy was not properly lighted. I am aware that an investigation was held and a report made, but possibly the minister
[Mr. Law.J
might give some concrete information on this important question.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Cobequid ran ashore on what is known as Trinity ledge. Before running ashore on Trinity ledge the ship passed close to the Nova Scotia coast and to the eastward of the Lurcher Shoal lightship. The statement was made that the Lurcher Shoal lightship was out of order and that the light was not burning. Such was not the case. The light was burning. It is a most modern light. The fog alarm was in perfect order and also the submarine bell, but in the fierce storm which was prevailing at the time the submarine bell was probably of not very much value. Although the light was burning, and although the fog alarm was in perfect condition, the steamer was not attracted by these signals and ran on Trinity ledge. It was far out of its course. The finding of the wreck commissioner about the matter was that the captain, after he had seen the light from the Nova Scotia coast farther down, should have stayed out to the westward in the open sea, because, if he had done so, the accident would not have happened. The gas buoy that marks the* Trinity ledge was not burning. These buoys go out from tune to time, and when they do the fact is reported to the agent of the department in the district, and the practice followed is that notices are published in the newspapers in the different ports, and notices are also sent to the Canadian Shipping Federation. The object of publishing these notices is so that vessels in port may be made aware of the fact that a particular light is out of commission, and, in addition to that, the agents of the steamers will be able tp send wireless messages to their steamers, which they know are on their way to the port. This buoy was reported out of commission to the agent of the Marine Department in St. John six or seven days before the wreck of the Cobequid, and the agent immediately published the notices, and notified the Shipping Federation of Canada. The usual steps were taken, and when the wreck occurred the Landsdowne had a buoy on board taking it to replaee this buoy. The opinion expressed by the wreck commissioners, which no doubt is correct, is that the fact that the light was not burning on the buoy in no way contributed to the accident.

If the buoy had been
there, would it not have been an advantage to the captain to have seen it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understand that he
could not have seen it. The captain swore on the inquiry that in the storm that was raging it was impossible to see anything beyond the bow of the 'boat. Captain Lindsay, the wreck commissioner, told me-and I asked him most particularly on the subject, because I was naturally anxious about it and interested in it-that if the light had been burning it *could not possibly have prevented the accident, considering the nature of the storm which was raging at the time. In :any ordinary weather, the captain would have seen the light on Lurcher, or he would have been warned by the fog whistle, but the men in my department who have been sailors, or who have been in the navy, tell me that conditions arise now and then when aids to navigation will fail. Such were the conditions prevailing outside the bay of Fundy when the Cobequid went on the Trinity ledges.
I understood the minister to say that the submarine bell was in *operation at the time of the wreck, and I am curious to know if .the ship was [DOT]equipped with submarine apparatus?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The submarine bell was in [DOT]operation and in perfect order on board the lightship, but whether the Cobequid was [DOT]equipped with submarine apparatus or not, I do not know. I asked that question -of Captain Lindsay, but apparently that information was not given. Captain Lindsay, however, expressed the opinion to me that even if the Cobequid had been [DOT]equipped with the apparatus to enable her under ordinary conditions to get the sound of the submarine bell, it is doubtful, considering the storm, that it would have been effective on that occasion.

When these submarine bells were introduced a great deal was expected of them and considerable expenditure was entailed by their installation. It would be interesting to sea-going people to know what results we are getting from them. I hope the minister will ascertain whether the Cobequid was equipped with this apparatus or not, and if not it would be well, perhaps, that these subsidized vessels should be so equipped. I understood that the captain missed his way to some extent, due to the fact that the lightship had been out of commission some short time before, and that he did not know it had been re-lit when he was entering the bay of Fundy. It is said that had he
known the lightship was in operation and lit, he would have had a better chance of getting safely into the bay. The only criticism I have to make, is, that it is curious that the Lurcher should have been out of commission very shortly before that, and that then when the Lurcher got into commission, the buoy should have been out of commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The utility and efficiency
of these submarine bells is evidently recognized by marine authorities, because at the recent convention in London, for the safety of ships at sea, one of the clauses of the convention agreed to by the thirteen nations represented by men of experience was that all lightships and important light stations should be equipped with these submarine bells. A good many \veek3 before the Cobequid came up the bay, the Lurcher lightship had been undergoing repairs. Once a year these lightships have to be taken from their stations to be overhauled and put in thorough order. Several weeks before the Cobequid sailed from the West Indies for St. John, the agent of the steamship line had been notified, through public notice, that the lightship was again in commission, and there could hs no excuse whatever for the captain assuming that the lightship was out of commission. The agent of the vessel had ample notice and time to communicate the fact to the captain of the Cobequid before he sailed from the West Indies.

The minister is quite
right in stating that the captain of the Cobequid made a mistake in not running for the Lurcher, but as he supposed the lightship was not there he did not make for her. On the other hand, the department is somewhat to blame for not having the buoy in order on Trinity ledges. I understood the minister to say that on this night it was so thick and stormy that the light would be no good, but I always supposed that these buoys were to be useful on just such occasions, for, on a moonlight night, when the captain can see all around him, there would be no necessity for them. I understood the minister to say that this light had been out for only six or seven days, but I would like to inform the hon. gentleman that after I put the question on the Order Paper early in January I had this letter from a captain:
Port Maitland, N.S., January 24, 1914. Mr. Law:
Dear Sir,-In reference to your question con-

cerning the light on buoy on Trinity ledge being out of commission, at the time the steamer Cobequid wreck occurred, 1 would say: Yes, it was; it has been out since the first heavy gale in December.
The Cobequid did not go ashore until January 13.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I remember the facts now. The light was reported out to the agent at St. John on the 7th January, and on the. 13th, six days afterwards, the Cobequid went ashore. '
But there is reason to believe that the light may have been out since the 1st December.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It may have been out, but the agent of the department at St. John was not aware of it; it was not reported to him until the 7th. I can readily understand, of course, a state of things under which a light might be out for a number of days without the fact being reported to tfhe department, for it might be that no vessel would pass during that time. But as soon as the report of the light being out was made to the' agent, he advertised the fact and took all the precautions usually taken in similar cases.
Mr. LAW..: It seems to me very strange that this light may have been out for nearly a month. What system has the department for getting reports on these buoys? This is a very important light, for it marks one of the most dangerous reefs on the coast, and my information is, though I am not a seafaring man, that had the light been in proper position the night the Cobequid was lost, she might have picked up the light and so not have gone ashore. I am glad that the minister, in reply to a question of mine, stated that it was his intention to duplicate the Lurcher light. It is certainly dangerous that that boat should be on the station eleven months of the year and then taken off a. month, and I am glad that a relief boat is to be sent. I think this case demonstrates the correctness of what I stated the other day. If the hon. gentleman kept one of his steamers, now at St. John or Halifax, in the port of Yarmouth, the buoys on these different ledges off that coast and at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy could be looked after and attended to much more promptly than at present. I can quite understand that a light on one of these ledges might be out some little time. It seems from what this gentleman writes me that this light must have been out for nearly a month. I think the minister should take the matter up and devise some
[Mr. Xjaw. i
means by which when these lights are out the matter shall be reported. This gentleman is a fisherman of Port Maitland, and they are fishing off that coast nearly every day. He goes on to say:
The buoy on the ledge had also drifted very close to the rocks and held there. If you need me to prove this tatement, I am ready any time.
If that was the case, I think tire department is subject to some censure. While I am on this subject I would again bring to the attention of the minister the matter of rewarding the captains who saved the crew of the Cobequid. It is going on two months since that matter was taken up. Has it received the proper attention of the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend speaks'of the system under which the department learns when these lights are out of commission. That system is the same as has always prevailed, and I do not see how there could be any other. The agents of every steamship line are requested to notify their captains to immediately report if they find any buoy out of position or any aid to navigation not properly discharging the work it is intended to do. In addition, all fishermen, as a rule, know that they are wanted to report these matters. As a rule such reports come either from steamship captains or from fishermen. I think that every man who traverses the sea recognizes the great value of these aids to navigation, and realizes the duty resting on him to report at once to the department if he finds any aids to navigation out Of order. And wben such a report comes to the department it is at once investigated. I understand the Ihon. gentleman to say that he has a letter from a gentleman who is a seafaring man. I do not know whether this gentleman speaks with .personal knowledge or not. If he does, and if he knew that the light was not burning, it seems to me he was not doing his duty to the public when he failed to notify the department. I can imagine a case where a light might be out of commission for a number of days without the department being notified. Aill we can do is, as soon as the department is notified, to take prompt steps to have the difficulty .rectified. I cannot believe that that light was out of commission for a month and nobody report the fact, for I should tnink that any seafaring man would report it at once. The Government has no vessel to scour the waters to see that the lights are. in commission. And, as I say.

the system in use seems to be the only possible one. It is one which has been followed with fairly satisfactory results for many years. The hon. gentleman asks with regard to rewards for the captains of the John L. Gann, and the Westport, the officers of which acted in a gallant manner in rescuing the people from the Cobequid.
I told the hon. gentleman that forms would be sent to him to fill up, and gave instructions to the officers of the department that that should be done.
I have not received any forms.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I think I stated in the House that that should be done, and asked the officials of the department then present to make a note of it.
I think the hon. minister refers to a form which I asked for, and which I received.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have asked the deputy minister to make a note of this matter, and I will let the hon. member for Yarmouth (Mr. Law) know to-morrow in what position it stands.

I am sorry to say the captain of the Westport was quite seriously injured while he was engaged in rescuing the passengers and crew of the Cobequid. He was thrown across a berth, and two of his ribs were damaged and other injuries inflicted, and he has been obliged to give up the command of the steamer. I really hope the minister will take the matter up as- soon as he possibly can. I see that the business men of St. John have recognized the bravery of these masters and their crews by getting up a purse and presenting it to them. The board of trade of Yarmouth has done the same thing; I forwarded to the minister a copy of the resolution passed by that board. It seems to me the Government, the largest body of all, should recognize in some very substantial manner the heroism displayed by these gentlemen.

I hope the minister will understand that I had no object in view in bringing up this discussion except to get his statement of the facts of the case. Not being a seafaring man, and not knowing very much about these matters, I yet venture to say that I am somewhat surprised that the Department of Marine and Fisheries itself has no way of keeping track of these light buoys. I had supposed that there was a regular inspection of them. I know that these buoys are supposed to run for weeks or perhaps foxmonths, but it would seem to me that, if they are of the importance one would suppose them to be, some system of regular inspection by the officers of the department would be adopted.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, the
buoys are inspected regularly. The lights are supposed to burn for a certain number of months, and within that period the steamers of the department visit and examine them, and charge them with the illuminating element. Between times, however, these lights often go out as a result of a heavy storm or the machinery getting out of order. We have the record of one light burning fourteen months, but the ordinary time they are supposed to burn is much less than that. However, the light may go out at a time when the steamer is not available. Between the border of the state of Maine and the Gaspe coast we have 5,000 miles of coast line to attend to, and the hon. gentleman will readily see that .while regular visits of inspection are made, the trouble may often occur between the regular trips. As a matter of fact, considering the great number of buoys, the trouble in that regard is comparatively rare.	,

Any one who has had
experience with acetylene gas lamps knows that accidents will happen to them, and I am not finding fault. I realize that these lamps are supplied with sufficient power to enable them to last a certain number of hours. I realize, too, that the Government steamers cannot be sent around the coast every week, but would it not be possible, without any very serious expense, to have a report upon each of these gas buoys at least once a week? I know I am speaking entirely as a layman, but it does seem, even to a landlubber, that if these buoys are to serve the purpose for which they are intended there ought to be some systematic method of inspecting them.
I understood there was a duplicate buoy at St. John at the time the news reached the department that the light on the buoy at the shoal was out; am I correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Quite correct.
And that the Lansdowne was at St. John at that time, that the news was received on January 7, and that the accident took place on January 13?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

The buoy at the mouth of the Bay of Fundy is within a few hours' sail of St. John, and any accident to an important buoy like that ought to be looked after at once. I do not think we should exonerate the officer in charge from any blame for not having taken prompt action, because, if he had the buoy ready and a ship at hand to take it out, he had ample time to attend to the matter before the accident took place on the 13th.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not at all surprised that that should occur to my hon. friend; the same thing occurred to me. When I learned that the facts had been reported on the 7th and that the buoy had not been attended to by the 13th, the inquiry I naturally directed to the officers of the department was why the buoy had not been placed there sooner. The reply I got was that these buoys are very large and very heavy, weighing about 16 tons, I think, and if the weather is 4 p.m. rough it is impossible to take the buoy off the boat which carries it out and place it in position without incurring the danger of smashing the ship and causing loss of life. At this particular time the weather was stormy and the water very rough, and the officials, rightly or wrongly-though, I think, rightly -decided that they could not take that 16-ton buoy out and place it in position till better weather prevailed.

I have no doubt that seafaring men and fishermen report accidents to the buoys in a great many cases, as they are probably more interested in the matter than anybody else. At the same time, however,
I daresay many of these fishermen do not know to whom to report that a light is out or a buoy out of place. For instance, if a fisherman saw a buoy out of place and the light out, would he be justified in telegraphing collect to the agent of the Marine and Fisheries Department at St. John?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly. We should be only too glad to have him telegraph collect, giving full particulars. My deputy tells me that the department pays the fishermen and others for time they may have lost in going to a place where there is a telegraph office in order to communicate the facts to the agent. Sometimes the buoys actually break away and are picked up and brought into port, and of course the department has to pay salvage. One of our buoys which broke away from its anchorage in a storm was picked up yesterday, I understand, in 
the vicinity of Boston harbour. It might be interesting to know that some years ago a buoy in the gulf of St. Lawrence broke away and nothing was heard of it until about two years afterwards, when it was-picked up on the coast of Australia.
I should like to repeat the question I asked the minister on February 5, as to whether a lightkeeper has been appointed at St. Esprit Island, county of Richmond?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the light of which Mr. Finlayson, who resigned, was formerly in charge. I cannot say that the appointment has actually been made, but a report has been .made to Council and a man is in charge of the light. I will ask my deputy to get the information for my non. friend.

Can the minister tell me
whether the man who is in charge is to be appointed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The inspector of lights
tells me that his- name is Ferguson, and that he is now in charge of the light.

Upon the resignation of Mr. Finlayson, I suppose that in the ordinary course of events the department was communicated with and a nomination requested by the person having the control of the patronage in the county. It was found difficult to make a choice between two rival applicants, and the matter was referred to a sort of election. They had all the excitement and paraphernalia of an election contest in the district; each can-'" didate was asked to get up a petition and the applicant who received the greater-number of signatures was to get the light. They were both Conservatives, and I think after the election was over the man having the minority of votes protested the election upon the ground that the Grits of the district had taken part. However, the retiring lightkeeper cut the knot by selecting one of the applicants and putting him in his place as acting lightkeeper. Very considerable interest is rife in the community as to the outcome of this election, and that is why I am anxious that the minister should be good enough to tell me what is to be the result of the polling in that district.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We will have to send for
the returning officer, or the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery.
Any box missing?

I am afraid that the vote
would not stand the test usually- applied to elections.

Could the minister tell
us how many Liberals have been dismissed among the lightkeepers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I could not say that offhand.

Could he tell the number of lightkeepers who will be paid out of this item?
* Mr. HAZEN:	The number of lights in
Canada in 1911-12 was 1,372, and the number of fog signals 289. Adding these together would not give exactly the number because in some lighthouses there are more than one keeper, and in some cases the work of a lighthouse and fog alarm are combined.
Has the minister at hand the number of appointments in two years?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
In making new appointments has the minister sent any notice or warning to lighthouse keepers not to take an offensive part in elections?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The instructions to lightkeepers are exactly the same as they were before the change of Government.

In my constituency, with
two or three exceptions, all lighthouse keepers have been dismissed. Those who have been appointed were our most active opponents in the constituency, and they were in every case appointed because of services rendered to the party now in power. They continue to be as strong partisans of the party in power as they were. That is undesirable, because it creates an unfortunate impression on the public mind, especially among those who do not take an active part in polities; it provokes a sense of injustice because it is felt that one man is dismissed because he is a strong Liberal and another is appointed because he is a strong Conservative, one is dismissed for the same reason that another is appointed. It would be well for the department, in making new appointments, to let it be known that there is a custom in force in the department that offensive partisanship will entail dismissal. In my constituency this would have a salutary effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The instructions are exactly the same as they were.

Who is the agent on
Scatari island? The reason I ask is that I am instructed that of the agents in charge of the Scatari lighthouses for fourteen or fifteen years, Captain Martel was asked to resign and Captain Pope was dismissed. Captain Pope went through a sort of mock investigation and was dismissed but Captain Martel was asked to resign or otherwise he would be dismissed for partisanship. I understand that the department-had a man there named McDougall who, I am informed, was an absolutely incapable man. The department, with all the knowledge possessed by its technical officials, could not instil into him sufficient knowledge to enable him to look after the engineering work on the island. Then I understand that they have tried another man, a man from Gardiner Mines but he also was incapable of receiving instruction and so they appointed a gentleman from outside the county of Cape Breton. I think it is unfair for any department of Government to dismiss trained officials who have spent fourteen or fifteen years on this l'onely island and then to appoint untrained men only to find in the end that they were not able to receive sufficient instruction to take charge of the engineering. This is unfair to the person dismissed, unfair to the department and unfair to the public. If McDougall was not capable of looking after the engineering he should not have been appointed. I do not say that any serious mishaps resulted but one might have been caused. I have not the information to-day as to who the present incumbent is.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken in saying that Mr. Martel was dismissed by the department.

I did not say that; 1
said that Captain Pope was dismissed and Captain Martel asked to resign or he would be dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Mr. Martel was not asked to resign by the department.
I can give the minister, inside of twenty minutes the letter to Captain Martel asking him to resign or otherwise he would be dismissed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Not at all; I am informed by my officials that charges were made against Mr. Martel, but before these charges were investigated and without any action on the part of the department to dismiss him, Martel resigned. He was not dismissed; he forwarded his resignation. In

many lighthouses the work is of an important character, as my bon. friend has stated. It is very frequently the case that when there is a vacancy a trained man cannot be obtained and the department refuse to appoint certain men recommended until they have had an opportunity of judging of their qualifications; and therefore it has occurred on many occasions that a man who has not the necessary certificates as engineer or the necessary qualifications 'by experience is sent to a lighthouse and an official is sent with him who has that experience, in order to ascertain if the man is qualified for the position, and if, after an experience of a few months, he will he able to fill the position. This course is frequently taken because of the impossibility of getting men on some occasions to go to these out of the way places who possess the necessary qualifications to look after the somewhat complicated machinery to be found in many of these modern lighthouses. In this case Mr. McDougall applied for the position and was sent there, but it was found that he had not the qualifications for the position, and therefore could not be retained. The light in no way suffered, because a competent man was there as well at that time and it was through this man that the department learned that McDougall could not qualify for the work. There are many cases of lighthouse keepers being appointed from outside the district or county whim there happens to be nobody in the district able to fill the position.
How much did they pay to McDougall for his services while they were training him ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know. In many cases these lighthouses are situated a long distance from other places and the lighthouse keeper has very little social intercourse with his fellowmen. The positions are not very inuch sought after. I think a Mr. Nearing is occupying the position at the present time. He has also to keep an engineeer for the purpose of running the station. In many of these lighthouses the man in charge has to engage an assistant or an engineer, selected by himself and approved of by the department. He pays him out of his own salary.
Who is engineer at Scatari island at the present time and where is he from ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know his name.

With reference to the dismissal of Martel, he probably took an

active part in politics-he admitted that- but never an offensive part. If he attended to his duties, and he always did, he would have no time to be an offensive partisan. But what I want to bring home to the minister is this, that the light at Scatari island, which was formerly looked after by Captain Martel, has been without a resident engineer for almost two years now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The information given me here by both the inspector of lights and the deputy minister, is that there has always been an engineer at the station.

That may be perfectly correct. Engineers have been sent there from time to time by the department, but that position has not been filled for two years. Mr. McDougall was sent there, personally a good man, I suppose; I have nothing against him, but a man utterly incapable of looking after that light. And let me tell the minister that after Mr. McDougall had been found incompetent to fill that position he was still allowed to have charge of the machinery for a certain time. Afterwards, Mr. McDonald, I think it was, came down from Halifax to instruct Mr. McDougall.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is some misunderstanding. The inspector of lights tells me that McDougall was never there alone. A competent engineer was always there to look after the machinery.

With all due deference to the source of my hon. friend's information, I can tell him that McDougall was in charge of the station when there was no competent engineer there. Mr. Nearing does not pretend to be an engineer. I want to point out to the (minister that this is the result of dismissing or asking to resign men who have given the Marine Department the very best service that is in them. When a government, I do not care whether it is a Liberal or Conservative government, begins to interfere with lighthouse keepers simply because they take somewhat active part in politics, I think they are making a great mistake; and if the department follows the recommendations sent in by the patronage committee, they are bound to get men in charge of those lighthouses who are not qualified. I can readily understand that almost any man can run an ordinary country post office, and fill most of the little Government positions that we have in our country, but when it comes down to lighthouses and a matter of safeguarding the lives of people

who of necessity must go upon the sea, then this department, or any other department that does it, is making a very serious mistake. I agree that the Government is justified in dismissing an offensive partisan, hut Captain Pope was not an offensive partisan. As a matter of fact, I think the recommendation of Mr. Duchemin in the case of Captain Pope was absolutely wrong. He was an old man of perhaps 60 or more, who had spent his life . on the island working for a very small salary. An investigation was held, but I think the minister himself should be the judge as to whether a charge of offensive partisanship has been proven. I know exactly what was proven in the case of Martel. He was a partisan, and had always voted Liberal -so far as I know. Captain Pope was also dismissed on the grounds of offensive partisanship when there was no evidence warranting his dismissal. The minister in my opinion should be the judge, especially in cases where the facts are not very strong one way or the other. I still maintain that considerable bungling has taken place in connection with the light that Martel had charge of, and I do not think the minister was fair to the people around the coast whose safety depended on this light, when he did not leave Martel in that position. We have hundreds of engineers in the county of Cape Breton who are qualified to take charge of this light, and who were well qualified to take charge of it from the beginning. The department must know that under our Nova Scotia laws it is an offence to put in charge of an engine of over ten or twelve horse-power any person who has not a certificate. The department must have known well enough that McDou-ga'ld did not hold a certificate when he went there, and I think it was a waste of money attempting to train a man for this position when we had lots of men in the county already holding a license to run engines.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The engineer who is there now has a certificate from the province of Nova Scotia. I do not for one moment question the sincerity of my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll) in regard to this or any other matter that he brings before the House; in fact, I have had reason, on more than one occasion, to think the contrary. My hon. friend has referred to the question of Captain Pope. A charge of partisanship was made against Captain Pope by Mr. Maddin, the former member, and who was a candidate at the last election. The mat-75
ter was investigated and this is the report upon which action was taken:
Mr. Duchemin was requested to investigate the charges, who reported on July 2 that he had held an inquiry, and that Michael Burke gave evidence to the effect Captain Pope had spent a considerable portion of the day about the same poll as he (Burke) was acting agent for the Conseravtive candidate. Captain Pope interviewed voters prior to their going in to vote. During the afternoon, witness went outside the poll and Mr. Pope there met him and said, 'Why not vote for reciprocity?' Witness replied that he would not vote in that way. Mr. Pope then said he was ' ready to bet money that the Liberal Government would be sustained, that if the Tories got in, all we would get to eat was corn meal and rye flour as when the Tories were- in before; that the Tories were
no d

good.' Mr. Pope also canvassed witness
at West Point Scatari during the last local election, asking him to vote for Kendall and Carroll, the Liberal candidates. Witness replied that he would not vote for them. William H. Campbell testified that he was a delegate to the Liberal convention, which nominated Mr. Alex. Johnston in 1908. Witness testified that Mr. Pope came in from Catalone to Sydney on the train with the delegates to the Liberal convention. Witness was unable to say whether Mr. Pope was a delegate at the convention hut admitted that Mr. Pope was present in the Lyceum in Sydney during the proceedings of the convention which nominated the Liberal candidate. For Mr. Pope to attend this convention he would take practically all day as he would have to drive five and a half miles from his home in Main-h-Dieu to Catalone, and thence go up by train 28 or 30 miles to Sydney. Mr. Duchemin accordingly found that Mr. Pope had violated the regulation of the department, in participating in election work. Captain Pope declined to give evidence himself.
If these witnesses were telling the truth and if, as stated, Captain Pope was actually canvassing at the poll-

How many voters were
there at Scatari?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know. If that is the T:ase I do not think there is any hon. gentleman in this House but will say that he could have no expectation of being retained in office.

The minister does not
know how many votes there were to canvass?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not know, but there
must have been enough to constitute a poll. I do not care if there were many or few; if Captain Pope canvassed for votes I do not think any one will seriously argue that he was not guilty of partisanship in the way contemplated by the Act which was passed in this House a few years ago and to which all members of the House gave their assent. It was about some such action

as that that an hon. gentleman, then sitting on this side of the House, said that if officials wanted to be politicians fche Government proposed to give them every oppor tunity to be politicians. That is practically the case with regard to Captain Pope unless my hon. friend from Cape Breton disputes the truth of it.
Yes, I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I understood the hon.
gentleman to say that Captain Pope was not an offensive partisan but an active partisan. I do not quite draw the distinction. If a man canvasses for any political party he is thereby taking his official life in his hand. I do not think any man will dispute that in such a case the Government is justified in removing that man from office. It may be that he may not do it offensively by shaking his fist under the nose of a man and telling him that he would or would not do a certain thing, but probably he is a great deal worse partisan than the man who does that.

What does the minister say about the two men in Truro who were enjoying a bottle of Scotch, drinking to the health of Macdonald, and somebody lying in wait under the window? Does he call that offensive or active partisanship?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would like to read the
evidence before venturing an opinion upon a mere statement of fact, if it is a fact. Those are the facts with reference to Captain Pope. Now I come to the case of Mr. Martel. Mr. Martel was not dismissed. A charge was made against him and he resigned.

I suppose the minister
would say that he would have been dismissed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would not say whether he would or would not have been dismissed on the report of the commission. But he resigned himself and, having tendered his resignation, we endeavoured to fill his position. I am not suggesting that my hon. friend is not absolutely sincere in what he has stated but the officials think he is mistaken in what he has stated about there not being a qualified engineer there. They state that there never has been a time when there was not a qualified engineer there.

I am not complaining very much about Capt. Pope's dismissal or about Capt. Martel's dismissal, but what

I do complain about is the way in which his place was filled. Capt. Pope came to me after he had got that summons notifying him that he was going to be investigated and he asked me to appear before Mr. Duchemin. I told Capt. Pope that it would be of absolutely no avail that I should appear before Mr. Duchemin, that my presence would not help his case, but that, as a matter of fact, it would injure it. He offered to pay me for going there but I said 'no.' I said to Capt. Pope: There was a young solicitor, a Conservative-not an offensive Conservative an I very many of them are not-who was practising his profession-Mr. Chipman. I said to Capt. Pope: Go and give your retainer to Mr. Chipman and I think that Mr. Duchemin will give him every consideration. I have no fault to find with Mr. Campbell's evidence given on that occasion although Captain Pope says that he never attended any convention to nominate a Liberal candidate in Cape Breton. He happened to be in Sydney on business of a private nature on nomination day with Mr. Campbell and Mr. Campbell probably thought he was there for the purpose of attending the nominating convention. I repeat that I have no fault to find with Mr. Campbell's evidence but I would like to point out to the minister that Burke wa3 an insane man at the time he gave his evidence.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
But Capt. Pope did not
contradict his evidence.

I will tell the minister
why he did not contradict it. Mr. Chip-man undertook to cross-examine this man, Burke, was at the time of the investigation an insane man.
When Mr. Chipman undertook to crossexamine Burke, he Mr. Chipman, was peremptorily told by Mr. Duchemin that if he would not hold his mouth he would pitch him through the window, or words to that effect. That took place in the early days of the investigation in the eastern part of Nova Scotia and as a result, Mr. Chipman, who is an absolutely reliable man-no friend of mine politically or otherwise except that we are good business friends-[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Who said that he would
pitch him through the window?

Mr. Duchemin told him that he was there absolutely on sufferance and that he would not allow him to crossexamine Burke. Then Mr. Chipman told

Captain Pope that it was no use for either of them to remain there and they both left the court together. This happened in the early days of these investigations. I am free to admit that Duchemin did allow counsel to cross-examine the witnesses after that during his investigations. These are the facts as told me by Mr. Chipman in regard to that investigation and I have no doubt they are absolutely true.

As long as we continue to run the Aids to Navigation of the coast along political lines we will have these difficulties and it is very unfortunate that trained men have to be dismissed for trifling reasons and untrained men put in their places. Something of the same nature happened in connection with Cranberry Island light. The lightkeeper on Cranberry Island felt uncomfortable after the change of Government. He was not dismissed but he resigned and it became necessary to put a man in his place. A man was recommended by the Conservative committee but he turned out to be incompetent. He could not pass muster before the inspectors, and his place had to be filled by some one from the outside.
Mr. Henry Hanlon, of Canso, a very competent man, who had several years experience, applied for the position. He had not much connection with politics, but his family happened to be Liberal. There was a petition in his favour, signed by those interested in the Cranberry Island light, and if the minister will look at that petition he will find that it is signed by scores of Conservatives. Mr. Hanlon was an excellent man and could have done the work most capably, but he could not get the appointment because the minister is running the lights on the coast on party lines. I do not refer to this to make complaint, but to ascertain who is in charge of the light station and engine on Cranberry Island.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: A gentleman named De Young.
Is he in charge of the light station and the signal station?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
Who is the engineer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He is the engineer; he has an assistant, whom he pays.
Has Mr. De Young been appointed permanently?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No; he has only been there a short time.
This is a very important station; has the minister made any arrangement to appoint a permanent official there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is a very important station, and that is why we have a very qualified man. No man would be put there who is not thoroughly qualified and competent.

I have had reports that I do not care to trouble the minister with just now, stating that part of the time since the late keeper retired the station has not been properly looked after. I have no information I am able to give him on that score, excepting, I would like very much to know that the minister is paying attention to it, and that he is looking for a capable man to put in charge.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The inspector of lights tells me it has never been an hour without a capable man in charge, and nobody will be put there in permanent charge who is not thoroughly capable.

I would like to know if the minister is sincere in his contention that he will take the lighthouse service out of politics. I wonder if he imagines that one out of fifty lighthouse keepers in remote parts of the country, have ever had an opportunity of reading the Lake resolution adopted by this House, with reference to officials taking part in politics.* Does the hon. gentleman intend to bring this resolution to the attention of the employees of his department, and put an end to this system which is demoralizing the whole service? I am speaking in the interests of the service, because I know it is useless to speak in the interests of those who have been dismissed; they will speak for themselves next election. Really, a change in the present system should be made by the minister. His officers should be notified that the moment they are appointed to office they should keep out of politics. In my constituency, the most rabid part'sans on the coast are now officials of the Marine Department, and they have been appointed regardless of age or qualification. I think the minister would revoke some of these appointments, if he really knew the truth about them. The gentleman who now recommends appointments in the county of Bonaventure, being a stranger to the county, my opponent having died last year, appointments of the most reckless character are being made, and they arc made not in

the public interest or in the interest of the department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
If I remember the resolution referred to by my hon. friend, it laid down the principle which justified the Government in acting in the event of officials taking part in politics, and it was not ;-the form of laying down instructions to officials. For my own part I do not think it is edifying to see public officials, occupying places in the Civil Service, tak ng an active part in politics on one side or the other. If they do so they know full well that they are, under the resolution of the House, taking their positions in their hands, and they will have no reason to find fault should they be dismissed, when a change of government takes place. Of course, the first essential which any government should look to, in appointing men to office, is their qualification, but there is no doubt that governments have taken into consideration in times past-and probably they will in years to come until you can get everything decided by some ideal system of competitive examination-the political claims of applicants for positions. Hon. gentlemen opposite did so when they were in power, and this Government is doing the same thing. But the fact that a man has been an active political worker before he assumed office, is no evidence that when he is in office he will continue to be an active political worker. In my own experience, on both sides of politics, I have known many eases in which men who had been extremely active in polit'cs have laid their politics to one side after being appointed to office; and have endeavoured fairly and properly to discharge their duties. When I became Premier of New Brunswick, I was pressed on -all -sides to make dismissals, but in most cases I refused be-caus-e I did not think it a sufficient reason that the gentlemen who were occupying official positions had been active opponents of mine before they were appointed. In nearly every case I found these gentlemen anxious to be loyal to me, as Premier of the province, as they would have been loyal to any one who occupied that position. I may say to my hon. friends opposite, who .are discussing this matter- fairly, that in my experience, as a rule, I found, with a few notable exceptions, that men who occupy official positions upon which they are depending for their livelihood, have abstained from taking an active part in politics. On the other hand, it is my experience that men occupying small

positions, such as keepers of lighthouses and small post offices, out of which they do not make a living but which are entirely subsidiary to the occupation which is their main source of support, are in many cases active politicians in the districts in which they live. In my own constituency, in the city of St. John, there are a large number of persons employed in the customs house, the post office, the inland revenue, the Department of Public Works, and other departments, but so far as I know they take no active part in politics on one side or the other. But when you get men in these small offices which do not give them a living, they apparently do not value them enough to keep quiet when there is a political contest on, and they are willing to take the chance of being dismissed. I understood my hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) to suggest that some instructions should be sent out.
I do not object to men being appointed for past political services, but I do say that when they are in office they should keep out of politics. .

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is my opinion.
Out of the twenty-five appointments in my county, I am sure that not twenty of these men ever heard of the resolution of the House about nonparticipation in politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: These men probably know, as well as my hon. friend and myself, that if they take an active part in politics and there is a change of Government, they may expect to lose their positions.
They are under the impression that if they do not serve the Conservative party they will be turned out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This is the same charge as has been made in the past about men who were Liberal partisans but who have sought to defend themselves by saying: We were afraid we should be turned out of office if we did not take part in politics. But I leave it to hon. members to judge to what an extent such an excuse was justified. I do not think it an edifying spectacle to see men drawing public salaries and obtaining their livelihood through public service taking part in, politics-, nor do I think it a desirable thing. But how does the hon. gentleman propose to remedy the state of affairs under which parties will naturally appoint to office men who, having equal qualifications with others, are active supporters of their party? That can only be changed when we

come down to saying that there shall be public competition for every office, a competitive examination by independent authorities, thus eliminating patronage from politics-and I think most politicians will be very glad to have it eliminated. Of course, to a very great extent, that has already been accomplished in the inside service. I know that in our department when we need officials we send to the Board of Civil Service Commissioners. They have a list of peoplo who have already passed examinations and from whom can be chosen the officers we need. Or, if the officers required are technical officers, those men are advertised for and applicants state their qualifications and a selection is made. Thus the question of patronage is largely eliminated from the inside service. But whether you can extend that to the fishery overseer or the postmaster whose salary is $50 a year is doubtful. Certainly, I doubt that the time has come when that can be done. I take the view expressed by the hon. gentleman, and I hope that when he was a Government supporter he expressed the opinion that he does now.

oome officials with salaries of $1,000 and thereabouts have been dismissed in Gaspe and elsewhere. The result has been to give a very bad impression of [DOT]the public service to many of the voters. I have about five thousand voters in my county, of whom about twenty-five are interested in these matters on one side or the other. A great part of the community look upon this dismissal of officials as demoralizing, and I think the minister should make some attempt to put an end to it 'by giving due warning that if a man wishes to hold office he must keep out of politics, and by assuring the official that he will not be disturbed if he observes the condition. I could name officials in Bonaventure who have been most active politicians since they have been appointed in their places. They are being rewarded by the Government for the assistance which they gave and the system which is so demoralizing is being encouraged. While I am on my feet, I should like to ask the minister if there is an age limit to the appointment of lightkeepers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None.
I thought there was such a limit established. Was there not an age limit in the old days?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

This Government has appointed one man of seventy-two years of age. Does the minister think it in the public interest that there should be no age limit, no condition as to whether a man is blind, or lame-

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think it desirable to appoint such people.
I made a recommendation, and the man was turned down because he was sixty years of age.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: He may have had other disqualifications.
No, he was a most respectable man and well qualified. Does not the minister think it desirable that there should, be an age limit in the appointment, of lightkeepers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think it desirable to appoint old men.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Does the
minister say that there never was an age limit for the appointment of lightkeepers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is my information from the deputy minister under the former Government.
In the form sent to me to fill out in such cases an age limit was fixed, and it was also made conditional that a man must be strong, healthy, able to row a boat, and so on.

I am in a position to [DOT]say that the Conservative Government, before 1896, did have a regulation fixing an age limit in these cases. I have a distinct recollection of correspondence, which the minister will find in his department, between the Minister of Marine of that time and Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper before he became Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper tried to secure the appointment of a man sixty-five years of age to the position of lightkeeper. The minister of that day stated that there was a regulation that a man could not be appointed permanently as lighthouse keeper after he was forty years of age. The correspondence went on, and the minister declined to accept the recommendation of his then colleague and appoint the man to office. And all through the period when our friends were in power, as my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) says, those of us who were consulted in regard

to recommendations know that the respective ministers in all cases insisted that a recommendation for permanent employment as a lighthouse keeper should apply to men under forty years old, and declined to appoint men who were over that age. If there is no regulation now, that means that there is no regulation since the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hazen) took office. Here we have another of the pledges contained in the Halifax Platform absolutely thrown to the winds. One by one these ethical and idealistic propositions which the leader of the present Government put before the people when he sought their confidence are being disregarded now that he and his friends have the responsibility of office. On Tuesday ,my hon. friend from Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) exposed the fact that the Prime Minister, who had pledged his word to return to the provinces of the West their public lands on fair terms, and had gone, through the western country promising that these lands 'should he returned, in addition to the subsidies that these provinces had received, to-day does not propose to do anything of the kind. He recedes from his position.

I desire to correct my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald): the Prime Minister's promise was distinct and absolute, and there was no such expression in it as 'on fair terms.' I could quote the words of the hon. gentleman: his statement was without qualification-that he would restore to these provinces their natural resources.

I had not the advantage of hearing the whole debate. But the hon. gentleman only accentuates the point and shows how far the Government is from attempting to fulfil its promises. Now, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries makes a frank acknowledgment on this question of appointments to office. The right hon. Prime Minister, with many an appeal to the high heavens to show his sincerity in regard to the matter, said that if the Conservative party were elected to office appointments to the Civil Service and to Government positions throughout the. country would not be made upon the grounds of party service, but solely upon the fitness of the applicants for the positions. And now, my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries comes along this afternoon and says that is not what he is doing. Of course everybody knows that is not what this Government is doing;

everybody knows that the condit'ons to which the hon. member for Bonaventure referred as existing in his constitu ncy exist almost everywhere else. In this connection the fact to be definitely remembered is that the discussion this afternoon discloses the positive declination of this Government to carry out another one of its pledges set out in the Halifax platform upon which the Conservative party went to the country previous to the last election.

The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) might have elaborated this idea and brought to the attention of the committee another declaration of principle which the right hon. Prime Minister has thrown to the winds, and that is the principle which guiided him in determining whether or not officials had departed from the fair and legitimate ground they should occupy in respect to political matters. The right hon. Prime Minister said in this House that, in his judgment, no man should be dismissed from office simply because he took part in politics. He said that officials ought to be permitted, as citizens of this country, to discuss political matters, and so long as they did not go out of their way to become offensive to their ministers or superiors in office, or to he uncivil towards the general public, they ought not for that reason to he dismissed from office. That is a principle upon which the right hon. Prime Minister was very emphatic a few years ago. .What is the spectacle that is presented to us at the present time? The hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries devoted almost half an hour this afternoon to defending the position which the Government has taken with regard to the dismissal of men who have been adjudged guilty of partisanship. For my part I never did and never will take the ground that a man who has been proved guilty of political partisanship ought not to pay the penalty of his transgression, so long as interference in elections is regarded as a transgression on the part of government officials. But what shall we say of the ease of a man who has been dismissed upon the alleged ground of political partisanship, when not a single tittle of evidence is produced to support the allegation made? In the name of justice and fair play, I protest against the Minister of Marine and Fisheries dismissing from public office not men who have been adjudged guilty of partisanship, but men whose offices have been claimed by greedy office-seekers.

In order that a vacancy might be created, *false charges of partisanship have been made against these officials, and these false *charges have been bolstered up by a commissioner appointed for that purpose. Does the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries forget that a year ago I called to his attention the case of Michael O'Brien, who was summoned by Mr. Duchemin to appear before him for investigation at a place called Port Malcolm, in the county of Richmond? Mr. Duchemin, in order to make it impossible for this man O'Brien to appear before him to answer to the charges made, held court eight miles away. The evidence adduced in that investigation, so far as I recol-5 p.m. lect, had reference to a conversation that O'Brien is alleged to have had on the road with a woman. O'Brien is alleged to have said that the *Government would be returned to power and that Kyte would be elected. Mr. Duchemin said in his report that inasmuch as that evidence had not been denied by O'Brien, he must have been guilty of making the assertion, and that he was, therefore, justified in recommending his dismissal. I called the attention of the hon. member to the fact that it was impossible for O'Brien to be present on that day to answer to the charge or to deny the evidence given against him, because he was sent on a false errand eight miles away from the place where Mr. Duchemin held his court. But the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries has done nothing to right that wrong; he has done absolutely nothing to reinstate Mr. O'Brien to the office from which he was dismissed. Therefore I say that the hon. minister is not doing himself justice when he gets up and undertakes to defend the conduct of the Government as regards the dismissal of officials who have been guilty of partisanship. What shall be said of the dismissal of officials who have been dismissed upon false charges, in respect of which no evidence whatever was submitted to justify their being removed from office? Take the case of Marin Bourque, which I discussed in the House a few days ago. He was summoned on September 28, 1912, to appear before Mr. Duchemin on a charge of partisanship. I was present at that investigation. A witness was called who could give no evidence of partisanship against this man Bourque, and I thought that that would be the last of the charge made against him and that he would be reinstated to office. But what happened?
Duchemin reported to the minister that when he went to River Bourgeois to hear evidence in the case, no witnesses were called; no one was prepared to give evidence with regard to the charge, and the matter was left open until a later date. Some weeks afterwards Mr. Duchemin returned to River Bourgeois. I was not present on the second occasion. There was no person present but Mr. Duchemin, the witness who sought to have Bourque dismissed, and another witness who was called in at that time. Bourque himself was ill, and unable to be present. His wife was told by Duchemin that he, Mr. Duchemin, came there for the purpose of taking a statement from Bourque. No suggestion that any further evidence was to be taken was made, but behind Bourque's back, under circumstances that made it impossible for him to be present, the same witness who was examined on September 28 and failed to give evidence of partisanship against Bourque was recalled, and in the presence of Duchemin alone, and in the absence of any person to cross-examine the witness or to look after Bourque's interests, Duchemin took the evidence of this witness and sent a report to the hon. minister. The statement made by Mr. Duchemin in his report that Bourque was adjudged guilty of partisanship is laughed at by every man in the county of Richmond wlio knows Bourque. When I discussed this matter the other evening I isaid that Bourque was absolutely incapable of being a partisan; he is a man who had no language in which to discuss political matters, and who was so absolutely indifferent to the success of the party that he only voted once, I believe, since he was appointed to the position of lightkeeper. There is the case of Bartholomew Boudreau, a man having a large family to support, whose health was not good, and who was ill-prepared to go out into the world and earn a living. His office was demanded by a person who thought that he had rendered sufficient service to his party to justify his demanding that reward. A farcial investigation was held by Mr. Duciiemin and Boudreau's lighthouse was handed over to the Conservative who sought the position. I say that of all the departments of the Government there is not one that standi on a worse eminence than that of the Department of Marine and Fisheries in respect to this matter of dismissals.
Post Office.

The Post Office Department is no worse, and when I make that statement I give hon. gentlemen some idea of how bad the record of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries really is.
Throughout the length and breadth of the province of Nova Scotia the conduct of the Department of Maxine and Fisheries smells in the nostrils of every right-thinking man. There have been more unjustifiable dismissals in the Department of Marine and Fisheries .than in any other department of the Government, except, possibly, the Department of the Postmaster General. The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) referred to the dismissal of an engineer having to do with the light at Scatari island, and the appointment of a person in his place who is not licensed or competent or qualified to operate the engine connected with the light. That is no new step in the record of this Government. The dismissal of competent licensed officials and the appointment of unlicensed persons in their places is not uncommon. Last year I called the attention of the House to the case of the dismissal of a school teacher in charge of the Indian school at Salmon river, county of Richmond. A young girl, a qualified second-class teacher, having a Normal school diploma, was dismissed, for what reason? Because she was a partisan? No, they could not make any allegation of that kind; but they appear to have rummaged around the graveyard and learned from the to)nbr stone erected on the grave of her dead father some suggestions that he in his lifetime was a Liberal, and she was dismissed on account of the political leanings of her family. Did they appoint a licensed teacher in her place? No, they took a young man, the son of a Conservative, who, according to the report of the school inspector on file in the department of the Interior, had neither license, experience, nor qualifications. He was appointed to the school in place of this young girl. Therefore, I say that if you take one department of this Government after another you will find in the matter of dismissals and appointments to office more conduct absolutely unjustified and unjustifiable than can be found during the forty'years of the history of this country previous to the advent of the present party to office.
I rose for the purpose of calling the attention of the minister to the fact that in December, 1912, I moved for a return

of the number of dismissals made in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Up to this hour I have never seen that return. I think the hon. member for Laval (Mr. C. A. Wilson) the following January moved for a similar return and has never received it. I think the time is opportune to ask the minister if he will not, while these Estimates are before the committee, produce a return containing the dismissals from his department up to the present time.

I do not know
whether the word ' sickening ' is parliamentary or not. For about three years now we have had a repetition of the case of this school teacher and other cases in Nova Scotia and other parts of this country in reference to the dismissals that have taken place since this Government came into power. It is nothing new. Any man who has been actively connected with the politics of this country knows very well that when there is a change of government *-I do not say it is right, but it is the condition that exists in this Dominion to-day and has existed for a great many years- there is an inclination that its friends should receive the public offices. I am not so very sure, although we hear a great deal of talk, that it is a very wrong principle after all. I am going to refer to my own constituency.
