I have been intending to do it when I have heard the hon. gentlemen on the other side talking about high morality, but I have refrained from stating this case, for two reasons. One especially is that in my own town the post office is held by two young ladies who are giving splendid service, who always have given good service. Although they are the descendants and the close relations of very active partisans of the late Government, I want to tell you that these girls' heads are safer to-day than they ever were when their friends were in power, without any question. What are the conditions in the constituency of Souris s Some of you may know that I have the honour of representing the south half of the constituency that used to be represented by the Hon. Clifford Sifton. The sentiments of my hon. friends opposite must have changed very much, because I do not think that Clifford Sifton was any better or any worse than my friends who sit on the other side to-day. There are about 70 post offices in my constituency. The Hon. Clifford Sifton began at one end, at the town of Pearson, and went to Elva, to Melita, to Boissevain and all through

my constituency to about 25 towns, and, with the exception of about four, every man or woman who held the position of postmaster or postmistress in my constituency was dismissed. What has been the record since this Government came into power ? Just four postmasters or postmistresses have been changed in that constituency. One used his automobile all day to carry voters to the poll, and the other was a very active partisan-a delegate to the convention that nominated the Liberal candidate. I was going to say that my hon. friends cannot be sincere in this talk which has been repeated and repeated so many times, especially by my hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte). In my own town, Boissevain, a town of about 1,000 people, the postmaster built, in the centre of the town, a splendid stone building simply for a post office. He was a man in whom everybody had confidence; the citizens felt safe in sending the smallest boy or girl who was able to walk to that post office to get the mail. Things went on until there was a change of government. This gentleman had been postmaster for a long time, but he was dismissed. My partner, who was a good Liberal, but none the worse for that, when I told him that they were talking about dismissing Alexander MeKnight, who was so far from being a partisan that you could not get him to vote at a meeting of trustees in the school district, who never voted for anything, he said;	' Oh,
no, they will not turn out MeKnight; our party do not do things that way.' Very well, MeKnight went. Who got the position? A man w'ho kept a hotel was appointed in his place. That was not the worst of it. Within about three months after he was appointed he had the posit office turned over to his daughters, and went to the next town, where he ran a saloon. What did our Liberal friends do? Something very similar to what I have heard talked about on the other side of the House. They were very much displeased; they were all going to vote against the Hon. Clifford Sifton the next time he came around. That settled him; they would not stand for that. They sent a very strong petition down to Ottawa, but nothing was heard of it. They went further than that; they had at my own house a meeting at which a splendid silver service was presented to Mr. MeKnight; they had a very nice time, and the Liberals were the principal speakers in condemning the Liberal Government for dismissing Air. MeKnight.
It seems to me that the Government has bad a tremendous lot of patience. I have a little grievance against this Government, and I think that the Hon, Mr. Pelletier is a sinner in some respects in this matter: he has not turned out the men in my constituency that he should.
Hear, hear.

When I tell you I have only asked for five out of seventy, it will be seen that I have not been very active in the matter. I do not know how these other members get their men turned out. I cannot be in with the Postmaster General as well as some others, if we are to believe what has been told on the floor of the House. If I want to have a postmaster dismissed the Postmaster General insists on an investigation by a so-called judge, and exceedingly strong ,evidence has to be adduced.
Has Mr. MeKnight been reinstated?

No, sir, he has not. That post office is being run by those two girls to-day, and there is not a single Tory in the district who would raise a hand to have them dismissed. They will be there just as long as they wish to be. Not one postmaster dismissed by the Hon. Air. Sifton has been reinstated since this Government came into power. I think the Government has had a great deal of patience in listening to the hot-headed speeches that have been made on the other-side, but I would advise the Postmaster-General not to take them too much to heart, for there is not much in them.

The hon. minister will remember that a few days ago, with a view to bringing about those ideal conditions in the outside service which he has extolled, I gave him the names of three gentlemen who were active partisans in the last election-I do not object to that-and who were continuing their offensive partisanship by attending organization meetings of the Conservative party. The hon. minister promised that he would instruct these officials to stop meddling with politics. I would like to know if these men have been written to.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They have not been written to yet; we were taking that matter up this morning.

I think the member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) has a real grievance

against the Postmaster General. Sometimes I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Souris, but I heartily agree with him in this case. I want to tell him what the Postmaster General did in my constituency. He did not ask for an investigation; no. About one week after they were installed in office, the postmaster at Woodstock, a town of about 4,000 people, was simply told to get out and hand his papers over to his successor. That is the way they do it in Carleton county; and all over Canada there was not a postmaster whose job was required by a Tory but was told ' hand your papers over to John Jones, and there will be an officer down here to-morrow to take your place.' Sometimes the official got notice by wire, and at other times the Postmaster General took time enough to dismiss him by letter. If the Postmaster General requires evidence of partisanship in the constituency of my hon. friend from Souris, I want to tell my hon. friend'that he has been unjustly discriminated against. It may be that the Postmaster General thinks my hon. friend from Souris is going to get his reward anyway, if they get certain legislation through the House. The Postmaster General can afford to be a saint in the constituency of Souris and a sinner in every -other place. If any other gentlemen have grievances against the Postmaster General, I think this is a good time to bring it up, because we can give so much evidence as to the way the Postmaster General conducts things in other constituencies.
Mr. A. De WITT FOSTER: I have listened to the very vitriolic speeches that have been shot across the floor of the House by hon. members from eastern Nova Scotia, and at this particular time I do not intend to take issue with them because I really do not think it is worth while.
Make an attempt at it.

The hon. member for Carleton is attempting to be facetious, but that does not worry me at all. I simply rise in accordance with the same right the hon. member for Carleton has, although I am pleased to say I do not do it so often and to so little purpose.
Thank God.

My last remark also applies to t'he gentleman who has just made that invocation. The more hon. gentlemen opposite pour out their vials of wrath upon 
the Postmaster General the stronger he is in the country. No man in the Cabinet has more of the confidence of the country to-day, in so far as I am able to judge from my own constituency, than the Post' master General, and I will add the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. Since they have taken office they have done things in the way of administration of which the people of the country are very proud. It is true they have dismissed some officials who were in office when they came in, but the country will only hold them responsible in this regard: they have not dismissed half enough in many -counties, and to strengthen their position with the electors they should rid the service of many more who (have no business	in the public service. If
there is one thing the public life of this country needs, it is !to be rid of the class of officials that was working for the late Government in the various constituencies, particularly of Nova Scotia. That applies to the county of Carleton as well.

The position that has been placed before the House by my -hon friend from Souris and by my hon. friend from Kings, N.S., is something that is entirely beyond the humorous. We have understood that the Government's responsibility was to give service to the Government through its officials. Our friends who have just spoken have -laid down the principle that the business of the Government is to find places for their political friends at the cost of the public treasury.
You laid that down yourself.

No, I did not lay it down either personally or by practice. I say that -such a principle laid down in this Parliament is something to cause the people of Canada to take notice. We do not object to the Government that has been recently installed in office making Changes to secure greater efficiency in the public service. There is something to -be said in favour of a condition whereby a new government, free from the associations under which officials then in office attained their positions, are able to exercise discretion in securing greater efficiency in the public service-a thing which the Government responsible for their appointment were scarcely in a position to do so well. That must be admitted and so f-ar as that is concerned, my friend from Souris and I are very much of a like mind. But when it comes to -a declaration that the Government of the day is weak-

ened in the country because it has not made public service a political reward pure and simple, then I say it is time for the Government to make a declaration on the subject and let the country know where they stand. And we will certainly have to ask the minister leading the House for a declaration of the Government's position on that point. If it is to be the position *laid down by his supporters so freely, the *country is entitled to know it, and if that is not the position of the Government, it is for the minister to say so. I was elected to Parliament in 1896-
Who laid down that declaration? It was your party. '
It was laid down in the Wagner case.

I was elected to Parliament in 1896 on the occasion of a change *of government. I had been offering for the support of the electors in the locality of Edmonton for some years as a candidate for the local legislature. I can say without hesitation that every employee of the then [DOT]Conservative Government of the Dominion had been an active political worker against myself both during my contests for the local House and during my contest for the Dominion House. I was elected to represent what is now practically the province of Alberta, and there was necessarily a very large number of appointees of the then Dominion Government rendering public service throughout that area which is now largely the province of Alberta. There was, as far as I am aware, throughout the province of Alberta, and certainly in the locality of Edmonton, no man dismissed because of his political opinions and, as far as I know, there was no man dismissed throughout the length and breadth of Alberta upon the accession of the Liberal Government to power unless there was some grave cause for their dismissal in the interests of the public service. While there may have been isolated cases of that kind, they were certainly isolated cases. I must take this opportunity of protesting against the sweeping assertion that has been made from time to time by our friends on the other side that they to-day are doing as their opponents formerly did.
I did just the opposite of what was done by my opponents.

I want to put myself on record as to the conditions prevailing in Alberta and as to the position taken by the
present Government. During the elections of 1911 there was not in the constituency of Edmonton any official of the then Government who took any part in the election-absolutely not. Officials were warned by me not to do so, and they did not do so, but immediately after the election the immigration agent at Edmonton was dismissed. Some time afterwards-quite recently-two other officials of the immigration hall were dismissed. Several of the homestead inspectors were dismissed.

Do you say that
they were instructed not to take part in politics?
Yes.

Did	you instruct them
personally?
Yes.

By	circular or written
notice ?

By written notice; every
official of the Interior and Indian Departments was notified, and I have reason to believe that a large majority acted in accordance with that instruction. But in the district of Edmonton, although the appointees of the Dominion Government did not take an active part in the elections, they were dismissed just the same. The immigration agent at Edmonton was summarily dismissed almost immediately after trie election without a charge at all and no charge could have been successfully made against him, either of political partisanship or inefficiency in the service. Who was appointed in his place?-The President of the Conservative Association in the city of Edmonton. Who was appointed in the place of one of the homestead inspectors?-a man pamed Brown. Perhaps it would be better to draw a veil over the results of some of these appointments, but shortly after this gentleman was appointed he was missing for some time and he finally turned ;up in the Red Deer Hospital suffering from an attack of D. T.'s and after some time further passed out of the service. The land agent at Grouard was dismissed, as far as I know, without any -charge against him at all. A man was appointed in his place by this Government whom 'they themselves had to dismiss a few months ago for improper conduct in the management of his office.

They did not promote
him.
No, they fired him.
But you did. You promoted a man for the same thing.
For what?
For stealing from immigrants and trifles like that.
My hon. friend will have to take that back right off.
It is admitted by-
I ask the hon. gentleman to take that- back immediately.
,1 did not accuse my hon. friend from stealing from anybody.
No, no.

But I say it has been
proven on the floor ,of this House and by the records of the House, and my hon. friend has not denied it, that Philip Wagner, a convicted thief, after his conviction and release Jtrom jail, took an active part in the elections, and was promoted by my hon. friend to a higher position in the Department of the Interior than he had held before his conviction.
I must ask the hon. gentleman absolutely to take his statement back. It is untrue and he must take it back.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It
seems to me that the words of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) have reference to a certain fact. I understand that if we attribute words to an hon. member of this House which are denied by him we must accept his denial. But here is a question of fact that I cannot judge of.
If I am not to have your protection, Mr. Chairman, and if it is necessary for members across the floor of this House to call each other liars, well then, we will have to do it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If such is the case, I understand that the hon. member (Mr. Boyce) is out of order. I understand the hon. member to state that a man outside of this House had some charges made against him, and that afterwards he was promoted.

The hon. gentleman has charged that I promoted this man, Wagner, after he had been convicted of a crime. I

say it is false, and I ask the Chairman to compel the hon. gentleman to withdraw the statement.

I am speaking of that which is not new at all. I am referring to something which took place, last session, and which was the basis of a resolution moved in this House. The facts are indisputable, and the hon. gentleman knows that they are true. I stated them because they are on the records of this House, and the statement I made was a fair statement, as the records of this House disclose.
Am I to have your protection or not?

The hon.
member (Mr. Boyce) has another opportunity of proving what he .says if he can; hut under the rule of the House he is bound to	accept	the
statement of my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), who declares that he did not do such a thing. A member's statement must be accepted or there is an end to the proceedings of this House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Since the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) denies absolutely having done such a thing, his word must be taken.

Take it back now.
Mr. .BOYCE: I will certainly accept the hon. gentleman's word if he feels that, having the record of - his previous statements in this House, which are in 'Hansard,' he can now state that the account I have given of his words and of all the facts is not a proper or a correct account. I am bound by the rules of the House to accept imy hon. friend's word now, notwithstanding that it is inconsistent with his previous statement and with all the facts as they are in the records of the House.
I must ask you, Mr. Chairman, to direct that the hon. gentleman must unqualifiedly withdraw the statement which he made, because it is untrue.
Withdraw it.
No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It seems to me that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyce) has explained his position and taken back the words as best he can.

No, he withdrew his statement with a qualification which I object to. I made an unqualified denial, and I

desire that my unqualified denial shall be unqualifiedly accepted according to the rules of the House.
I bowed to the ruling and submitted myself to- the Chair, but after I had done so f stated what my own impression was.
My hon. friend will now have to withdraw the impression.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Is not that going a little too far ?
It remains for the Chairman, according to practice, to decide if the statement made is a withdrawal, or not.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that the hon. member withdrew what he said, and he stated afterwards that his remarks had been founded on certain things. I do not feel bound to rule that the hon. member has not made a proper apology.

I can only say that if we are not to have the protection of the rules of Parliament in our debates, the consequence must rest upon the presiding officers and upon the Government side. We have had a very clear statement of what the rule is, and all I ask is that it be complied with. If members of the Op-' position are not to have that protection, of course we will have to carry on business as best we may. However, as we have your ruling, Mr. Chairman, I may be permitted to proceed and to say, that the appointments that were made, to the position of immigration officer at Edmonton, to the land agency at Grouard, and to the homestead inspectorship in place of Mr. Gordon Macdonald, were appointments made because of political partisanship. Men were appointed because they were political partisans, so that they would continue to act, at the. expense of the country, as political partisans for the party now in power.
The same as you did.
Again I must ask my hon. friend to permit me to say, and I will ask him to accept niy statement, that I did not do any such thing.
I did not say you personally, but I say it was done by your party, and the hon. gentleman must know it. The officials there were active partisans, and very active partisans at that.

I am only speaking of what concerns my own constituency, and of what I know, and I can say that this Government-whose policy has been declared today by its supporters as being weak and inefficient, inasmuch as it has not absolutely turned the public service into a political organization for the benefit of the Conservative party at the country's expense-has done that in the instances I have mentioned in my own constituency. If they have not gone far enough to suit these hon. gentlemen, they at least have gone far enough to discredit themselves in any profession they may make as to Civil Service reform, which, hon. gentlemen opposite will be good enough to remember, was one of the leading planks in the platform of their present leader when he appealed to the country, and not only when he appealed to the country but long before he appealed to the country, when he declared for Civil Service reform from his seat in the Opposition. We are bound to believe that the country took him at his word. They gave him the opportunity to carry out the professions he had made, and to carry out the policy he had professed, with tire result that not only does he not intend to reform the Civil Service; not only does he not intend to disassociate it from political partisanship, but, on the evidence that has from time to time been placed before this House by members on this side, it has to be admitted that there has been a carnival of partisanship in the Civil Service of Canada since the accession of this Government to power, such as Canada never saw before under any previous government.
That is a joke.

And not only that, but the followers of the party opposite state to-day that the Government is discredited because it has not gone further along that road.
Mr. SCHAFFNEil: I repeat that in some cases they have not.

I want to say that when the Liberal party were in office they gave the country efficient service, and they did provide a measure of Civil Service reform, so far as the Civil Service in Ottawa is concerned. The Liberal party gave no cause for the attitude that has been assumed by the Government and their followers towards the Civil Service of this country. I say that the conditions existing to-day must cause every Canadian to hang his head in shame.
Oh!

I am sorry if my hon. friends opposite are not ashamed, but when the leader of a great party, time after time in this House, makes a definite declaration of policy in regard to an important matter of the administration of this country's affairs, and then, on acceding to power, absolutely goes back on even the colour of the professions he made, and with the approval of those who attained to power on these professions, it is time for Canada and Canadians to hang their heads in shame.
Will the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question?
Yes.
I think he has made a very strong statement?
Yes,

If I understand the hon. gentleman aright, he referred especially to the inside service as being conducted by the late Government in this city in a non-partisan way. I say there are instances after instances where men have been promoted and put over the heads of other men, by the late Government, in the Civil Service of this city, because they were friends of the late Government. There is no doubt about that.

I do not say that the late Government administered the Civil Service without partisanship. What I said was, that they gave the country efficient service and that they did introduce a measure of Civil Service reform as applied to the service in Ottawa. But this Government does not seem to consider the question of efficient service. That is not the point with them at all. speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I think the hon. member
asked for the number of dismissals in the Department of Marine and Fisheries since

the change of government in 1911. When I came into office, the total number of employees in the Marine and Fisheries Department was 7,000. There have been 510 dismissals, or 7 per cent. When the Liberal party came into power in 1896 the number of officials was 2,600, and the number of dismissals 420, or 16 per cent. In both oases the dismissals are on the same ground, that is, on the score of partisanship and incompetency. The dismissals since 1911 have been entirely in what is called the outside service. There have been no dismissals in the inside Service, that is, in the department here at Ottawa. As something was said this afternoon which would suggest that an entirely different practice prevailed under the previous Government, .1 would just call attention to one case because I know more about it personally. I find that an investigation was held in 1896 in the case of B. R. Palmer, the lightkeeper at Palmer's Point, N.B. Mr. McAlpine was the commissioner appointed to investigate this charge and reported to the Minister of Marine that the charge was not satisfactorily proved. There is on file a letter from Hon. A. G. Blair, the then Minister of Railways and Canals, to Sir Louis H. Davies, in which, amongst other things, Mr. Blair, states:
Mr. McAlpine tells me that he reported the charge ' not proved.' If this is a correct statement of the result I would thinlc it most inexpedient to take further action against Palmer. Of course he has not been a political friend of mine; but I would think his removal ought not to take place on the ground of his being an offensive partisan, when it appears he was not such.
An Order in Council was issued dismissing Mr. Palmer, such order stating that it had been established to the .satisfaction of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that the keeper referred to was an active political partisan on the occasion of the last Dominion election.
In the case of Mr. J. P. Dillon, light-keeper at Whitehead, N.S., an investigation took place. Mr. Dillon was unable to appear owing to ill-health, but forwarded affidavits contradicting the testimony given before the commission. Mr. Dillon sent in his resignation, and Commissioner Douglas recommended that his resignation be accepted. The department declined to accept the resignation, and an order was passed dismissing him from the service.
' My hon. friend from Richmond (Mr. Kyte) referred to three cases of partisanship in Nova Scotia that were investigated,

the result of the investigations being that the commissioners reported the charges as sustained, and the .officials complained of being dismissed. My hon. friend has referred to all these cases before in the House.

Not nearly all. There
were eighty dismissals from my constituency, and I have not referred to half of them,

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend has referred to these three cases on previous occasions. He referred to one case last session and to the cases of O'Brien and Bourque this session. I do not think my hon. friend has given the House anything new with regard to them this afternoon, yet as they have been referred to I feel it only proper that there should go down on * Hansard ' the statements that have been made with regard to these cases from the departmental standpoint, and from the standpoint of the commissioner appointed to investigate them. I take first the case of Mr. Boudreau who was lightkeeper at Poulamon. This case was referred to Mr. Duchemin for investigation and he reported :
I find as follows:
1.	That Bartholomew Boudreau attended the
Liberal convention as a delegate in the summer of 1910.	.	.
2.	That he engaged in political discussions in a public manner among, the voters of Poula-mon that he attended the nomination meeting at Arichat in September, 1911, and subsequently engaged in an argument, and gave out very partisan accounts of the proceedings there.
3.	That while keeper of the light at Poulamon, he made public comment on the result of the last provincial election in the province of Quebec, endeavouring to establish that this result indicated that the Liberals would at an early date return to power in Dominion politics.
4.	That he indulged in very offensive remarks with regard to Mr. Gillis, the Liberal-Conservative candidate for Richmond county in the last Dominion election.
5.	That he has herein violated the regulations of the department prohibiting employees from taking part in elections.

Has Duchemin submitted
the evidence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have not the evidence
here. I presume it is on file in the department. It is hardly necessary for me to refer to the case of Mr. Bourque. I only do so that the two cases may be side by side on ' Hansard.' Mr. Duchemin's report in this case was as follows:
Mr. Bourque was duly notified of the time and place of the hearing, but his wife appeared and stated that her husband was not well enough
to be present and that he did not intend to be present anyway. She was advised that her husband could either appear at the inquiry or see Mr. Duchemin during his stay in River Bourgeois, when he (Mr. Duchemin), -would be pleased to submit the evidence taken against him, and transmit to the department anything he might have to say. Mrs. Bourque, however, assured Mr. Duchemin that her husband did not intend to appear at all, and he did not.
Testimony was given by Wm. J. Levisconte, merchant of River Bourgeois, and Wm. Boudreau, master mariner of the same place. Mr. Levisconte testified that he had known Marin Bourque for years and declared that he had always been a most objectionable Liberal partisan. He further testified that in the Dominion election of 1908, when the campaign was in progress that Marin Bourque used most objectionable language towards the Conservatives, calling them 'that dirty party' and saying that 'I would never vote for that dirty party'. Mr. Levisconte added that while Bourque was not a .man that exercised much influence in the district, he had nevertheless always been offensive and objectionable as a Liberal partisan.
Wm. Boudreau testified that Marin Bourque had always talked of politics openly in a 'nasty and insulting way'. In the 1908 election, he (Bourque) had come to him and told him that 'he was a fool to be working for that party' (meaning Conservative) because they were going to get licked anyway. Mr. Boudreau also stated that Bourque had always been openly offensive when elections were taking place.
Mr. Duchemin found that Marin Bourque had been an offen3ive partisan and on this ground his services were dispensed witn.
(Mt. KYTE:	Is there not a report from
Duchemin in respect to a former investigation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We discussed that the
other night. The third case was that of Mr. Michael O'Brien, lightkeeper at Bear island, Nova Scotia. After briefly reading the finding of Mr. Duchemin, I will explain the point that was taken last year by my hon. friend, and to which he again referred this afternoon.
Mr. Duchemin's report was that:
1.	Michael O'Brien left Bear island and took away the only boat belonging to the lighthouse, arid went down to Arichat and attended nomination proceedings, being absent for a day and night from his lighthouse.
2.	On the day of the provincial election, held in June, 1911, Mr. O'Brien, although a perfectly literate voter, caled out in the polling booth the name of the candidate for whom he intended to vote, and insisted upon the presiding officer openly marking his ballot for him, stating that he was claiming to have this done, because he was a Government official.
3.	Mr. O'Brien used offensive partisan language on election day in the presence of Mr. Alex. Malcolm, a voter at Port Malcolm.
4 Mr. O'Brien has thus offended against the rule of the department prohibiting employees



from taking part in elections, and has also been guilty of offensive partisanship.
My recollection is that last year my hon. friend (Mr. Kyte) took the ground that Mr. O'Brien had never been notified and had been given no opportunity to appear and make 'his defence. After the discussion in the House I, that night, mailed a copy of ' Hansard ' containing what had been said in that respect to Mr. Duchemin. On May 31, I received this letter from Mr. Duehe-min:
Sydney, N.S., May 31, 1913.
Hon. J. D. Hazen,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Ottawa, Canada.
He Michael O'Brien, lightkeeper, Bear island, Richmond county, N.S.
Dear Sir:
I am to-day in receipt of copy of the unrevised edition of 'Hansard,' for Friday, May 23, 1913, and note that at page 11022 et seq., Mr. Kyte, of Richmond, has made certain criticisms of the investigation which I held into the conduct of Michael O.Brien, lightkeeper at Bear island, N.S.
I shall not to-day traverse the many misstatements which Mr. Kyte has made in connection with this matter. It is quite evident that he has been most grossly misled by his informants in this connection.
I wish, however, to deal with what I consider the one serious criticism made in this connection, namely:-That the accused lightkeeper did not receive adequate notice of the time and place of the investigation, and that he was consequently not able to present himself thereat. Mr. Kyte points out that Mr. O'Brien was notified to appear before me at Edward Malcolm's house at Port Malcolm, on February 20, and that the investigation was not held there at all but that it was held at the Farquhar house at Port Hawkesbury, some four or five miles distant, and that it took place-not on the 20th-but on the 22nd February. He also read a statement from the accused lightkeeper to the effect that my original notice to him was not received by him until the day of the investigation.
The facts are as follows:-On the 17th of February, X mailed Mr. O'Brien notice to appear before me at Port Malcolm, at the house of Edward Malcolm, on the 20th February, at 2 o'clock in the afternoon. In due course of mail, this letter would have reached Mr. O'Brien on the 18th of February-two days before the inquiry. It so happened however, that the greatest snow storm of the season occurred at this time, stalling the trains, making the roads impassable and for a day or two preventing the mails from going to and fro regularly. When I found this out, and was satisfied that Mr. O'Brien could not have got the notice in time to attend the inquiry, I wrote him on the 19th or 20th of February, from Port Hawkesbury, and sent the notice to a Mr. Malcolm at Port Malcolm, for personal service on the lightkeeper, notifying him of the cancellation of the first notice which I had mailed to him, and requesting him to appear before me at the Farquhar House at Port Hawkesbury, on the afternoon of Saturday, February 22. In the same letter, which I sent to Mr. Malcolm, I enclosed subpoenas for 
witnesses. On the afternoon of the 22nd the witnesses appeared, but Mr. O'Brien did not. I made careful inquiries and satisfied myself that Mr. O'Brien had been served with the notice, and that he was purposely absenting himself, and then proceeded with the investigation.
The investigation, as you will note, took place on the 22nd of February. 1 did not make report to you in this matter till March 3-some nine or ten days later. There was certainly ample time for Mr. O'Brien to write me, explaining what prevented him from attending. He had received two notices in tne matter, and did not respond to either of them, either personally or by letter. Had he written me, and given any valid reason for his non-appearance, I should certainly have done, what I have always done in such cases-make arrangements for him to appear before me, see the records, showing the evidence of the various witnesses, who gave evidence against him, and make what statement he wished in his own defence. After waiting for a period of ten days, however, from date of investigation, and having been assured by those present, and who were certainly in a position to know, that Mr. O'Brien had been served as promptly as the witnesses themselves, I felt quite justified in sending forward my report to the department on March 3.
I can assure you that in all these cases I have taken every precaution when the accused has made default at the investigation, to satisfy myself that he had really decided not to present himself at the hearing, and I do not think there is the slightest question that in this case Mr. O'Brien deliberately absented himself from the investigation in question.
There are other misleading statements made by Mr. Kyte during the course of the discussion on May 23, relating to an investigation in another department, which I shall deal with at once, and shall state the facts correctly to the minister concerned.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) H. P. Duchemin,
Commissioner of Inquiry.
I thought it only right that I should submit to my hon. friend and the committee this statement in regard to the matter which I did not have when the question was under discussion before the House. These are the three cases that my hon. friend has referred to. They have been repeatedly discussed in this House on previous occasions as well as to-day and 1 thought it was only fair, in view of my hon. friend's return to the attack on the investigation that this statement should go on ' Hansard ' side by side with the remarks that my hon. friend has made.

In regard to the report of Mr. Duchemin in the case of Mr. Bourque, Mr. Duchemin 'held an investigation on the 28th September. He summoned as a witness William Levisconte, who was unable to give any evidence to sustain the charge against Mr. Bourque. What did Mr. Duohemin report to the minister? He reported

that although the investigation was held no -witnesses were examined. That was an absolutely untruthful report, and that report having been sent in, the minister ordered a second investigation, and we have Mr. Duchemin's second report. I presume the minister would be justified in accepting without any qualification the report made by his commissioner were it not for the fact that his conduct has been impeached so frequently in this House and that proof has been presented of the unreliability of his reports in many instances. In regard to the case of Mr. O'Brien, I read a statutory declaration from the lightkeeper himself in which he denied having received the notice sent to him by Mr. Duchemin until the day after the investigation. Mr. Duohe-min, in his letter to the minister, states that Mr. Malcolm was called to give evidence in the investigation. This is the same Mr. Malcolm to whom Mr. Duchemin alludes as having sent a copy of the notice of the investigation to, and this is the same Mr. Malcolm who wrote to the Minister of Public Works alleging that Mr. O'Brien was a strong Grit, and that he was a strong Tory and that, therefore, he was entitled to Mr. O'Brien's lighthouse. At t'he investigation the only witnesses who were called were Mr. Malcolm, the applicant for the lighthouse and his wife. I asked the minister if he had the evidence on which Duchemin bases his report, and he said he had not. Of course, if he has not the evidence to give me it is impossible for me to verify it. My recollection, from reading the document last year, is that this man, Malcolm, who was an applicant for the lighthouse, a few days after the change of government asked for it on the ground that he was a strong Tory and that O'Brien was a Grit, was the sole witness exceipt Malcolm's wife, and Malcolm is the lightkeeper appointed in O'Brien's place. Duchemin says he sent a special notice to be served on O'Brien. So we have the spectacle in this country of a man being put on trial, and practically the only witness called against him is the msn who is himself seeking the office of the person whom he is seeking to have dismissed, and upon this unsupported testimony the Minister of Marine and Fisheries acts. It is unnecessary for me to say to the minister that no court in the land would accept, to support even the most trivial offense, the testimony that is offered in these investigations. And, when a charge of partisanship is made against an official, which if proven involves the sacrifice of 761
his means of livelihood, it is about as severe a penalty as can be imposed upon a man, particularly a man who has a large family to support. Therefore, I say that the evidence upon which these dismissals are made, is absolutely inadequate and such as would not be accepted in any court of law. With regard to the case of Boudrot, the minister did not have a copy of the evidence either, but my recollection is that the witness was the man who was subsequently appointed lightkeeper, and who had every incentive and every desire, of course, to make the case as strong as he possibly could, irrespective of what facts might be brought out in cross-examination. With respect to the case of Bourque, he did appear at the investigation on the 28th of September, but when the second investigation was held in December, he was in bed and unable to leave his house. It was absolutely impossible for him to meet his accusers, and furthermore, his wife was assured by Mr. Duchemin that no witnesses were to be examined, and that he came there solely for the purpose of getting a statement from Mr. Bourque-himself.
Referring to the statement as to dismissals which the minister gave to the committee, I wish to ask him if the number of dismissals given in that statement, as having been made by the late Government, covers the whole period of the fifteen years they were in power ?

The whole point we have been trying to make on this side of the House, is, that the comparisons that have been made with the condition of affairs in 1896 do not exist to-day and did not exist in 1911. The Conservative party have to face this question from a different standpoint altogether from that which the Liberal party had to face in 1896. The Liberal party came in not pledged to reform the Civil Service; they came into office in 1896 under an old system that had grown up under the different changes of government which had taken place since Confederation. But the Conservative party, through its leader, had for a number of years prior to 1911 given clear and distinct pledges to the people of Canada that if they were returned to power they would effect reform in the Civil Service. It is not fair, therefore, to compare what happened in 1896 with what happened in 1911. In order that there may be no dispute in regard to the pledges given by the Conservative party let me read from the platform of 1908 and also from the platform of 1911 on the essential points that refer to this question of the Civil Service. I wish to place this on ' Hansard ' so that it may be available for hon. gentlemen opposite who wish to study the situation of their party on these matters. The platform of 1908 is, no doubt, familiar to hon. gentlemen on the other side. I have a copy of it here. It contains the picture of the leader on the front page.
Hear, hear.

It is a very good portrait. Let me draw attention to the fact also that it bears his signature, and he becomes responsible for everything within these covers. Now, look at the first clause in regard to the Civil Service:
The character of a government may be judged by its appointments to important and responsible public positions. An Administration which appoints dishonest or disreputable men to the public service, or retains and promotes officials who have been proved unworthy, cannot be credited with good intentions. '
Hear, hear.

That is a good principle, and I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite to study it in the light of the appointment of Morine and Landry. Now, on another page of this document, I find this reference to the Civil Service:
Appointments by Merit:	Appointments of
public officials upon considerations of capacity and personal character and not of party services alone.
Hear, hear.

I would like my hon.
friends opposite to square that with some of the revelations made here this afternoon.
I myself drew attention to a case at Canso where a position was vacant for which it was practically impossible for the Conservative party to And a qualified man. They have practically admitted that, because for several months the position has been vacant and the minister stated to-day that it was not filled but was occupied by a temporary employee. The position is a responsible one, the keeping of Cranberry Island light at the southern entrance to the straits of Canso. The man recommended by the Conservative committee has been turned down by the officer of the minister as unfit for the position, yet the oflice has not been filled because they could not find a suitable man. A gentleman applied for the position with whom no fault could be found, one who had had seven years' experience in that particular light, and who knew all about managing the lighthouse and the engine. This man had the endorsation of over forty leading Conservatives in Canso, but because he could not get the three men who control the party as a committee to sign his recommendation the minister would not appoint him. There was no other reason that could be mentioned why Mr. Henry Hanlon could not occupy this position except that he was a Liberal. I want hon. gentlemen opposite to read this declaration in their platform that appointments to the public service are to be made on merit alone, and try to square it with such cases as this and the hundreds of others that- might be given. Then, in this Halifax platform there is the following clause:
Civil Service Reform.
4.	A thorough and complete reformation of the laws relating to the Civil Service so that future appointments shall be made by an independent commission acting on a report of examiners after a competitive examination.
I understand that the Commission for the inside Civil Service was appointed prior to the election of 1908, so that the leader of the Government, when he penned that
clause, must have had reference to the outside Civil Service. What has he done to carry out his pledge to put the outside Civil Service under a commission? There is another platform, a manifesto to the people of Halifax, dated Halifax, N.S., August 31, 1911. This manifesto says:
Three years ago you elected my colleague, Mr. A. B. Crosby, and myself, to be your representatives in the Parliament recently dissolved. Then, as now, the demands upon my time denied me the opportunity of holding any meetings in my constituency or of meeting the electors personally.
Upon the great issue which has precipitated dissolution, and upon other important issues now presented for the determination of the people, I have issued an address to the people of Canada which X submit for your consideration.
Notwithstanding the enormous expenditure upon the National Transcontinental railway, little has been done to solve the transportation problem for Halifax. This port should become the real terminus of one or more great railway systems reaching into the prairie provinces and thence to the shores of the Pacific.
Cheer now. This is from the leader of the party that has been degrading the National Transcontinental railway, changing the grades so that Halifax will never have any use of it. (Reading):
The position and natural advantages of Halifax entitle it to that status. It is not necessary to enlarge upon the benefits which would thus ensue to the constituency and to the province.
It will be my aim and policy to accomplish this result.
I pointed that the way he is redeeming that pledge is by destroying the National Transcontinental railway-by making it useless as a great transcontinental route from the prairie provinces to the sea. (Reading):
Railway extension through the eastern part of the county has for many years been urgent. For fifteen years the federal Government with abounding revenues has remained indifferent and inactive. During the past session, while both federal and provincial governments were trifling with the question, I took the ground in Parliament that the road should be built as a part of the Intercolonial railway and without delay. As a result of this the federal Government has apparently been awakened to a momentary sense of its duty and an item oi $1,000,000 has been inserted in this years Estimates for the commencement of the work.
In that clause he tries to lead the electors of Halifax to believe that he was the man Who started the Musquodoboit railway through the county of Halifax, when everybody knows that he had nothing whatever to do with it. (Reading) :
The highways through the country districts of this and other counties have been for many years and are now in a disgraceful condition.

The time has come when the federal Government should co-operate with and assist the provincial governments in the establishment of a system of permanent state highways.
Hear, hear.

This policy which is outlined in my general address will be of vast advantage to this county, which has suffered so long in this respect.
Now, I am going to give something which my hon. friends from Nova Scotia, no doubt, will cheer for:
The fishing industry, so important to our province, is carried on largely by boat fishermen. The conditions governing boat fishing have changed greatly of late years. Fishing is now frequently carried on many miles outside of our territorial waters and during the entire year. The boats employed are more expensive, better equipped and more costly to operate than those in general use some years ago. Thus, boat fishing has become largely a permanent employment, and those engaged in it are in reality seamen. This change is advantageous to the industry, because it ensures a regular supply throughout the year, which is essential in order to retain our hold on the markets. The Liberal-Conservative party has adopted and will carry out the policy of extending to the boat fishermen the same free medical aid and attendance afforded to those employed on Canadian vessels engaged in the deep sea fisheries.
Hear, hear.

The cheering on that is rather faint. (Reading):
Before the close of the campaign I hope to have the privilege of addressing you upon these and other important questions.
In conclusion, I desire to pay a well deserved tribute to the energy, the zeal, and the industry with which my colleague, Mr. Crosby, has faithfully discharged his duty as your representative. He has been prompt, active and earnest on all occasions to safeguard and maintain the interests of his constituents.
Faithfully yours,
R. L. Borden.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that Mr. Crosby, after receiving that 9 p.m. recommendation, could not get elected. In the election of 1911, the main manifesto was a large document dealing with the question of reciprocity chiefly, which I will not trouble the House 'with reading. It winds up with a certain number of pledges which I think ought to be placed on ' Hansard ':
The pledge given by the Liberal-Conservative party.
The Liberal-Consdrvative partly gives its pledge to carry out the following policy if returned to power:

1.	A thorough reorganization of the method by whicq the public expenditure is supervised.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) cheers that sentiment. He has been called upon on various occasions during the present session to stand up for his old principle of tender and contract, but he has been very quiet on that subject. It has been revealed to him that the same old policy in reference to the giving of some contracts without tenders is carried out, and not the slightest change has taken place following the pledge of his leader, on which he received the votes of the people. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman should cheer that sentiment after the record his party has made for the past two or three years.
Give us one or two cases of contracts let without tender.
The Transcontinental.

I am not aware of any important contract let without tender. On the contrary, every contract on the Transcontinental was let after most public advertisement inviting tenders from the whole world, and in every case to the lowest tenderer.

The hon. gentleman misunderstood my question. He complained that on this side of the House I failed to stand up for the principle I advocated when on the other side. I am asking him to give us some contracts which were let by this Government without public competition.
We have done that already. Several ministers have admitted that they let contracts without tenders.
Give us the name of one. The hon. gentleman says there are many, but one will do for the present; let him name one.

I could give you a hundred. (Reading):
2.	The granting of their natural resources to the prairie provinces.
You will note, Mr. Chairman, that there are no such words here as ' on terms ' or ' on fair terms.' The Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) criticised the speeches made on this side of the House, saying that we were not stating the case fairly when we did not say that this handing over of the natural resources was to be made on fair terms. If hon. gentlemen will read this document-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am afraid the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sinclair) is not confining himself strictly to the item under discussion.
In order to get at all the facts in regard to promises relating to the Civil Service, I wish to put all the:e pledges on record.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: As much as possible, I would like the hon. gentleman to confine himself to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

speakerposition: subtopic
speechtext: ['As much as possible, I would like the hon. gentleman to confine himself to the Department of Marine and Fisheries.']

I think the minisleT
must have forgotten to answer the question I put before six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: What was the question?

What attitude does the minister propose to take in respect to his officials? Is he going to permit them to be
active, offensive partisans and not ccl 11 them to account? And what is going to be his attitude towards officials whom he has left in power and the officers appointed by himself? Is he going to give them a free hand, apart from these excesses, when they are in the pay of the Government, to go around the country looking after the revising of lists, acting as agents at elections and paid partisan officers in the conduct of elections? Is he going to permit them to take any part in election matters? Or is he going to keep them down to the business for which they are paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think my hon.
friend was in the House this afternoon when I told the House that I did not approve of officials taking an active part in politics. I think it is an act of impropriety on their part to do so and if my attention is called to officials of my department who are taking an active part in politics I will see what steps can be taken to check them. There are, of course, in the department temporary officials who, I suppose, do not think that their liberty of action ought to be curtailed because they are getting a few dollars from the department without permanent appointment. 1 am referring to those who may he regarded as permanent officials of the departm nt, and I think it is an impropriety that they should take an active part in elections, although, of course, they have a right to vote the same as anybody else.
How does the minister distinguish between permanent and temporary officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
Does the minister say
that an official appointed by Order in Council who is a fairly permanent official in the department, does take an active part in elections in the future, he will have the matter investigated and if it is found that the official has transgressed at all he wdl remove him from office?

If my attention is called to any case of that sort I will communicate

with the official, inform him what I have heard and warn him not to take an active part in the future. No instructions have ever gone forth, as I understand, from any government to officials to that effect; but if, in view of such a statement and warning, any official continues to take an active part in politics and the charge is repeated against him, I will have the matter investigated and deal with him.

I think the minister realizes the point I am making. It is all very well to say that if his attention- is called to the matter he will warn the official. We know that these acts take place during the elections, and you have no opportunity of asking the minister to warn the officials because you do not know until the act has been done. Will my hon. friend go so far as to warn this particular class of officials at the present time or before an election that they must not take any active part in -elections? In my constituency I have no fishery officials except a few of the class whom the minister has excluded.
I have a few fishery overseers appointed by the month, and I have no objection to the minister appointing his friends to that position. In New Brunswick my friend knows that at every provincial election-there has been no Dominion election since my hon. friend assumed office-every one of these officials is an out and out partisan. We had an illustration in Fredericton three weeks ago, when officials publicly went to the court house, took a part in the nomination proceedings and such things as that, and publicly canvassed at the polls. I would like the minister to declare some policy in order that we may know just where we stand. It is of no use to say 'You were guilty when in power.' If we were guilty we were punished. We want to know if he and his oolleagues will attempt to carry out the high ideals expressed by his leader, as the hon. member for Giuysborough has pointed out. These were high ideals and many people believed him. From the conduct of his party since we know that if he was sincere then he has had a change of heart since, or else he has been overpowered by the other sections of his Government. I give the Minister of Marine and Fisheries credit for wanting to be fair. Will he or will he not now lay down the principle and notify his officials, en bloc, that they must cease taking an active part in politics?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend has asked me a direct question, and I shall give him a direct answer. No government of Canada -has ever issued any instructions of that sort to officials. To do so would be to cast a certain suspicion about men who are appointed and are presumed to discharge the duties of their offices in good faith, and I am not prepared to issue any such instruction to my officials. Why did not my hon. friend impress that on his own friends when they were in office if he is so sincere to-day? My hon. friend must remember that in politics, as in other things, a good deal depends on whose ox happens to be gored. As I told my hon. friend in all sincerity, I do not think it is a proper or *edifying thing for officials of the Government to take an active part in political campaigns, and if officers of my department do that, and my attention is called to the matter, I shall try to apply a remedy to prevent it recurring. That is as far as I am prepared to state to my hon. friend to-night.

I am sorry the minister has not seen fit to go a little further. It only bears out the impression we on this side of tihe House have had in the last two years that his leader was not able to impress on his colleagues that degree of sincerity for these great reforms for which we and the country gave him credit prior to the election of 1911. I thank my hon. friend for being as fair and upright in the matter as he .has been to-night. He has stated the policy which we believe to be the policy of the Conservative party, that is he locks the door after the horse is stolen.
Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says,
' Hear, hear.' I know from some personal knowledge of the hon. gentleman that those are his sentiments. If there is any man in this House who will say hear, hear, to anything politically crooked, it is the hon. gentleman from Kings, N. S. We have seen that gentleman for two and a half sessions and I think if he stays another session he will then vanish from the political horizon, never I hope to re-appear.
Mr. Chairman,-

If my friend the guardian of all the Indians in Canada will just possess himself in patience for a while, I may tell him I have a little Indian matter in my constituency which I shall bring up at a later date. I am just giving him notice

that Indians are being pilfered from down there and their property is being taken away. But I am talking now to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. I am somewhat surprised that my friend did not go a little further, because the net result of his statement here to-night is nothing. He simply says that if he is returned after the next general election and you call to his attention the fact that certain officials are dabbling in politics he will take it into consideration. He asked me what we did. The moment we touch one of our friends opposite they come back with ' what did you do.' I will tell him what we did not do. We were not hypocrites who claimed a policy we did not carry out. Before the elections of 1896, 1900, 1904 and 1908, we did not preach to the country that we were going to reform the Civil Service cr that we were going to revolutionize the body politic of Canada, as did my hon. friends opposite. My hon. friend says he thinks it is a degrading, or at all events not an elevating spectacle, to see public' officials taking part in political contests. I agree with him, but the difference between us is that when a man takes the smallest possible part in a political contest my hon. friend ruthlessly cuts off his head. I think my hon. friend has degenerated since he came to Ottawa. It is to his credit that when he was made Premier	of New Brunswick in 1908 he did not carry on the carnival of	decapitation of
public officials as he has done since he became a member of this Government. He took what I think was the proper course down there. Very many officials were dismissed but hundreds were not dismissed by my hon. friend, and when he came to Ottawa we certainly had better opinions of him than his course has led us to entertain at the present time. I think he has fallen under the baneful influence of the hon. gentleman who sits to his left, and also of the gentleman who sits' to his right. I am afraid it is a case of evil communications, because my hon friend certainly was not possessed of that bloodthirsty spirit prior to 1911, which his friends have compelled him to exhibit since he became a member of the Government.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
I found that in the
Post Office Department.

You cut off every head. You left no living tree that you could get your axe into, and when you could not get evidence to dismiss a man, you dismissed him *without evidence. You d'smissed the fatherless, the widows and the dead. From the standpoint of Opposition members, I do not know that you are hurting us very much.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Why do you complain so much?

Every official that, you
turned out of office, will be a splendid election campaigner at the next election. I do not believe in this principle, and as proof of my sincerity I may say that I had the patronage of the county of Carleton in my hands from 1897 to 1911, and so far as I can recollect only two men in the county were ever dismissed from office for political partisanship. One was a collector of customs who took an active part in politics; he had been chairman of Conservative political meetings, had made political speeches and been as active a partisan as any man could be. The other case was that of a postmaster who did not remain in his office, practised his profession and had other people to do the work of his office. I do not say the office was not properly conducted, I think it was, but the other members of his profession fell that it was not a fair thing that he should enjoy a salary of $3,200 or $3,500 a year and employ others to do the work for which he was appointed. So he was removed from office. Those are the only, two instance, so far as I can recollect, where men were removed in my constituency for political partisanship during those 14 years. I do not say that I was not importuned by party followers right down to 1911, to have charges laid against certain Conservative politicians and have them dismissed from office, but I did not do it, and some of those men are alive to-day and still retain their offices. Election after election they had been active canvassers for the Conservative party, but I did not ask to have them dismissed from office, and I do not regret it, because as a rule they were persons occupying unim-. portant offices. Take a man in charge of a post office getting $33 or $40 a year. Do you mean to tell me that that man has not a right to exercise his franchise in this country ? I think it is carrying politics to a contemptibly low level to say that a man occupying such a position has not the right to exercise his citizenship and manhood in this country, or that if he does exercise those rights, it is at the risk of losing his office.
They only got $10 before 1896.

They get 835 now. I could cite instances of postmasters getting 8500 or $600 a year who continued active partisans down to 1911. I remember seeing one of them dancing like a wild man around a bonfire on election night, but we did not dismiss him, and I think we have the respect of the people of the country for that. I think if my hon. friend would take the course we took, he would feel better to-night, because I know the Minister of Marine is not carrying out his own ideas and views of what is right as between man and man in carrying on this carnival of decapitation of office holders.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: These are not my estimates; I suppose my turn will come later, but this is the second time the hon. member for Carleton has taken upon himself to state in this House that I have dismissed every postmaster in his county. At the tail end of the first session of Parliament he assured the House that I had dismissed every postmaster in his county.

That is not true; you will find it on ' Hansard,' but I did not
say it.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I was in my seat here and I heard the hon. member make the statement. I was sure that it was not correct, but my hon. friend was very, very angry, and I thought I would wait until the next day when he would be in a better humour to give him a chance to rectify the statement.
I think it was two nights before prorogation.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
Yes, at the tail end of the session, when I had no chance of correcting it. My hon. friend said I had beheaded every postmaster in his county, and he says now that he did not say it. I heard it with my own ears, and it is on ' Hansard,' so we are two to one. He has repeated it to-night. He says I have cut the head off every postmaster in his county.
I suppose he will be surprised when he reads that statement on ' Hansard ' tomorrow. These statements are misleading. I suppose I am using a parliamentary word when I say that ?
My hon. friend the Postmaster General has dismissed every postmaster in my constituency who is a Liberal and who had an office yielding-

So he did in mine.
Mr. CARVELL-$50 to $75 and over, and in nearly every instance without an investi-

gati-on of any kind. I cannot, at the present moment, recall -more than one instance where he even attempted to give these people a chance to defend themselves. In one instance a gentleman named Armstrong, the postmaster at Greenfield, had a chance to defend himself, but as far as I re-collect, these postmasters were simply told, with two days' notice, to get out and hand over their books and papers to their successors. If that is my hon. friend's sense of justice and fair play, I am quite willing that he should have it.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: My 'hon. friend -should not make those statements.
I understand what I am talking about, and my hon. friend will have a -chance to reply.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: It will all be in ' Hansard ' to-morrow.

I know it will be in
' Hansard ' and if it is any comfort to my hon. friend to hear it, i may say that it was only the little fellows who were getting $32 a year who were not dismissed; I am willing to give -him that little bit of comfort. He did not dismiss those postmasters because lie -could not get any Tories in the constituency to take their places. It was 'because no Tory office-seeker sought the position that he did not disturb the occupants. In every case where they wanted the head of an official the Postmaster General granted it, and he- granted it, if necessary, without an investigation or without giving the official a chance to defend 'him/self. If there is a sinner in the whole crowd of them it is the Postmaster General. If there is a man in the- whole Government who has no right to stand up and defend himself it is the Postmaster General. If there is a member of this Government who has violated every principle of what is fair and just between the Government -and the office-holders it is the Postmaster General. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries at least tried to cover his tracks, because I do not think we have any evidence of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries maliciously firing men from office without at least giving them a farcical investigation. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries .is a good lawyer, he 'has an idea of what looks right to the public, and while I think many of these investigations were a mere farce, still the minister i-s able to stand up and read from his records and say that Mr. D uchemin "gave these officials an investigation. Of -course, that is tantamount in many cases to no investigation at

all. But the Postmaster General 'has no such documents as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Oh, yes.
No, he has not.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Oh, yes.

No, he has only a letter from the defeated candidate, or the memorandum, or the patronage committee, saying that they want the head of John Jones; the Postmaster General immediately complies and off comes the head of John Jones.

He did not even send
them an affidavit.

That is what occurred in at least half a dozen cases in my constituency and he did not even send them an affidavit to swear to. He did not even give them a chance to answer his letters, he did not give them a chance to say whether they were guilty or innocent, he simply sent telegrams saying: turn over your books and papers, and in forty-eight hours they were dismissed from office.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I did not do that.

I do not think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries wants the Postmaster General to butt in and defend him. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is quite capable of looking after himself. He is not at all in the same class as the Postmaster General. He has some justification for his conduct and the Postmaster General will do his friend a good service if he refrains from dragging in the Post Office Department at the present time. We will have something to say to the Postmaster General later on.

It is really amusing
to hear the remarks which have fallen from the lips of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat in view of the record of the Liberal party. Everybody who knows anything of that party knows that when they came into power in 1896 they cut off the heads of, not hundreds, but thousands of Conservatives. In the province of Manitoba and throughout the West men were removed from office on the receipt of letter from the defeated candidate, or the elected member, without any justification. Men were removed from highly-paid offices as well as from the minor offices. The postmasters in the riding of Selkirk, as well as in the adjacent counties, were changed without any cause except that they were Conservatives. My hon. friend would like to get the
ministers to commit themselves to a policy which would not allow one of these officials to take any part in politics and in the next breath he advises the Government that the postmasters, who are poorly paid, should be allowed to express their opinion. How consistent the hon. gentleman is ! The hypocrisy of hon. gentlemen opposite is so apparent that it must make the public laugh.
Order.
Oh, go on.

My hon. friend over in the corner (Mr. Lafortune) must be suffering; he says that some postmasters were dismissed from his county. I can only say that if the postmasters who were dismissed in the hon. gentleman's constituency were as deserving of dismissal as a great many in the western constituencies the Government have not dismissed half as many as they should have dismissed. The complaint made by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House against the hon. gentlemen sitting on the Treasury benches to-day is that they have not dismissed men who ought to have been removed from office for active partisanship, and not that they have removed too many. There is not one case in the West where men have been removed from office who were not active partisans. In my own county I had several cases where men were active partisans and I have no hesitation in saying that I recommended the minister to remove these men. Some of them were removed and I take the full responsibility for their removal. But it amuses me to hear the statements of the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat. He came into this House in 1907 with a very respectable majority, but his majority fell away until last time he saved himself by about seven votes and if he continues to exhibit the bad temper which he has displayed here tonight his majority will be diminished altogether the next time he appeals to the electors. I did not intend to say one word; I asked the hon. gentleman a courteous question and I received the answer I might expect to receive from a man that I would hardly consider worthy of a seat in this House, not from a gentleman who is sent here by his constituents to treat hon. members of the House with that courtesy which one gentleman would expect from another. The exhibition we have had to-night from the hon. member for Carleton, N. B., illustrates what has been said at different times on this side of the House of the rank hypocrisy of

hon. gentlemen who have been preaching ever since we came into office about the hardship that it entails to dismiss these men who have been active partisans and who, when they were in office, dismissed men right and left without any reason. I remember that in my own province there were one hundred officials dismissed inside of ten days after the change of government took place in 1896-I will not say without any justification, because I presume these men were party men-but if such treatment was good for these men, then surely hon. gentlemen, opposite should not complain about it now. I would not agree to the Government committing itself to a policy that would say that a Government official must not take any part in politics, and if he did that he should be removed from office. This was not the policy pursued by the late Government, and ought not to be adopted by this Government.
The hon. gentleman tried to induce the minister to notify the officials, that those who were in future guilty of partisanship would be removed from office. Does not the non. gentleman know that the late Government distributed a circular amongst its officials, warning them not to take part in elections, and that that circular was simply, to my mind, a warning to these men to get ready for the campaign, because, in my own county, the men who received these circulars, were the most active campaigners I had against me. And, not one of these men was dismissed. The late Minister of the Interior can bear me out tnat a circular was issued.
I did not say anything about that.

The hon. member
stated that the late Government had not warned the officials.

I made no reference
whatever to any such matter.
I understood the hon. gentleman to have endeavoured to induce the Minister of Marine to issue instructions.
That is rignt.
And I understood the hon. gentleman to say that no Government had ever done so.
I never said that.

The late Government did send out circulars, but, as I say, it seemed to be a warning to the officials

that they were expected to take an active part in the campaign. Personally, I do not approve of highly-paid officials becoming active partisans, but I agree that men who are occupying small offices should not. be debarred from taking part in politics. These men ought have a perfect right to express their opinions and to vote, if they want to. I say further, that when men become active canvassers and offensive partisans, no hon. gentleman on the opposite side can object to such men being removed from office. I do not believe any officials have been removed from office under the present regime, except those who have been guilty of partisanship.

I am .sure the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) is well qualified to lecture hon. gentlemen on this side of the House as to what the Liberal Administration should or should not have done with reference to partisan officials. The hon. gentleman is probably the only member of this House who is quite as well qualified as himself to take a high stand on the question of fair dealing with political opponents, because he furnishes the only instance on record in this House of a man having taken such a high position that he has even appointed Grits to office instead of Tories. I referred, a week or so ago, to the fact that my hon. friend had gone so far as to appoint the Grit returning officer in the last election to the important post of Indian agent in his constituency. I am sure the House must appreciate what a magnanimous and generous thing the hon. gentleman did in that.

Was there any reason
for it?

Evidently, the returning
officer at the last election in Selkirk must have counted the votes quite to my hon. friend's satisfaction, and, having done so well the last time, I should not be at all surprised if the hon. gentleman were to ask that official to step down from his official position when the next election comes around and again count the votes.
What was his majority-how much did the returning officer give him?

Eighty more than
you got; my majority was 87 and yours was seven.

You are wrong there;
my majority was more than seven.

The majority of the hon.
gentleman (Mr. Bradbury) was not so great that he has any particular reason to boast over the hon. member for Carleton.
