I do not think the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) felt so grateful to his returning officer, even though he was a Grit and the hon. member was a Grit, that he would attempt to do [DOT] any great service for that gentleman after the election was over. That is something my hon. friend from Selkirk can very well boast about. He can certainly stand on his high ideals and lecture hon. gentlemen on this side of the House after such a generous deed.* We, on this side, will be very much surprised if this gentleman is not further rewarded by my hon. friend, by being put back on the job he had last election for the time it is necessary to count the votes, and probably after that the hon. gentleman will have something still better in store for his returning officer. The hon. gentleman said that the Liberal Administration did send circulars to officials in Western Canada, and I can tell the hon. member-and my hon. friend from Edmonton can bear me out in this-that when the late Administration left office at least fifty per cent of the Dominion land agents in western Canada were Conservatives. Further, some of these Conservatives were appointed 'by the late Administration, and yet the hon. member tells us about the heinous treatment that was handed out to Tory officials in the West under the Liberal Government. The^e were men who were left in office for fifteen years, men who were known to be Conservatives in politics and partisans. One official in my constituency was appointed Dominion lands agent, although he was a son of Mr. Norquay, ex-Conservative Premier of Manitoba. The Minister of Marine said that no previous Administration had issued circulars or directions :to officials that they should not take an active part in politics, but the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) has contradicted him in that. I do not know whether the minister was referring to his own department or to all departments of Government, but I do know that the hon. member for Edmonton, when Minister of the Interior, issued circulars instructing his officials throughout western Canada not to take an active part in elections. I. have no doubt whatever, that some of these officials transgressed these instructions, but I will say that I consider that these instructions had a very great influence *on the conduct of officials, and that a great many were restrained from taking an active part in the elections, when possibly their
natural inclinations would have led them to do so. More than that, I say that the hon. member for Selkirk is going absolutely beyond the facts, and beyond any inference he has a right to draw, when he says that these instructions were apparently issued for the express purpose of being disregarded, and of apprising the officials to get ready for the elections. I do not think the hon. gentleman can take the list of the officials in the West, and say that they were not influenced to be non-partisans by these Instructions.
My own opinion was that they were less partisan than they would have been without these instructions. So, when the minister takes the position that he would be treading on new ground if he were to carry out the suggestion of the hon. memb;r for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), he is quite astray. He may be correct with regard to his own department in the past, but he is not correct with regard to every department of the Government. Whatever department of the late Administration might be open to criticism and attack for its treatment of officials of contrary political persuasion, certainly the Department of the Interior under that Administration is not open to such criticism as has been offered by the hon. member for Selkirk.

A stranger listening to this discussion and not knowing hon. gentlemen opposite would come to the conclusion that the Government of the day had been pretty busy since it came into office in 1911 dismissing officials in different parts of Canada.
That is no dream.
They are all Tories.

No, they are nearly all of the same political persuasion as my hon. friend-not all; I do not say that. But when you bring out the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite were in office for fifteen years and realize how many changes ike

place in official life in that time, it is easy to see that a large number of these officials must have belonged, and do belong, to the party of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Does not the hon. gentleman think these ten representatives are to be congratulated?

I am calling attention to the fact. But to hear hon. gentlemen opposite talk of wholesale dismissals, accusing the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. ,'Hazen) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), who is so bitterly condemned by the hon. member for Carle-ton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), one would think that almost every postmaster in Canada had been dismissed. [DOT]

I can tell the hon.
member that nearly every postmaster in my constituency who was supposed to be a Liberal was dismissed. I am not trying to make out a case; I am telling the facts.

The Postmaster General
took issue with the statement of my hon. friend. According to ' Hansard,' which the hon. gentleman now denies, the hon. gentleman made the wholesale statement, in the closing days of last session, that every postmaster in the county of Carleton had been dismissed. I am not going to discuss the matter further. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not wish us to enter too far into these discussions; they want us to wait, and I am on the waiting list.

What are you waiting
for?

For an opportunity. Hon. gentlemen, so far this Session, have been discussing small matters in which the public at large are not very much interested, and so hon. gentlemen on this side have not had much opportunity to take part in the discussions. We are going to give these hon. gentlemen plenty of opportunity-plenty of rope, if I may use the expression. I only wish to impress upon this House and the people that this Government has been very careful with respect to the dismissal of officials. I have given the figures with regard to ten counties. And were I to go over the whole province of Ontario, I believe the same proportion would hold good.

But I suppose the hon. gentleman will not be surprised to know that that state of affairs does not obtain in Quebec. There have been more dis-

missals in my own constituency than the hon. gentleman has spoken of.

And should none of these
officials have been dismissed?

That is not the point. I brought the matter up this afternoon to try to induce the minister to put an end to this system of dismissal-to warn those now in office to remain out of politics, so that they might remain in office when the Administration changes. But we have had no satisfaction from the minister on the subject. Of course, if these men display offensive partisanship, they will have to be dismissed, when the Administration changes. I do not know how it is in Ontario, but the system of dismissing officials prevails in Quebec and apparently in the Maritime provinces.
The hon. gentleman's leader made the statement in this House that each case must stand on its own merits.

I did not want to interrupt my hon. friend; we are old friends, and have sat here together for fifteen years. But I would point out that each successive government should be an improvement upon its predecessor. Now, the late Government introduced an important reform in placing the inside Civil Service under a commission, and we are looking to this Government to bring about improvements in relation to the outside service. -

I think if the hon. gentleman would ask tire Canadian people, they would say that this Government was altogether an improvement on the late Government. This Government is commencing a great reform, and they must be sure the foundation is good before they commence. When the foundation is absolutely secure-
When the Grits are all removed?	i

The hon. gentleman knows where the deadwood is. I apologize for having spoken so long, but I thought it only fair that some statement should be made during this discussion that would leave a fair and reasonable impression upon the public mind, showing that there were no undue dismissals, and that in many counties in Ontario not one official has been dismissed since this Government came into power.

That may prove only that the ministers were so busy dismissing

officials in the Maritime provinces that they have had no time to do anything in Ontario. We have had returns to show that dismissals in the department of the Postmaster General numbered about 1,100, and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has told us that he dismissed about 510. We have other returns relating to other departments which I think would bring the number up to a good many thousands. The hon. gentleman speaks of the six dismissals in ten counties, but in my own county eighty dismissals took place. And during sixteen years of Liberal Administration only two dismissals were made.
Are supplies purchased by tender and contract?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have a memorandum
containing the information my hon. friend desires to obtain, and I will read it to him. It is as follows:
Lighthouse supplies, ships' stores which are carried in stock at the different agencies, are purchased in the following manner: The agents prepare a list of their requirements for the coming year which are forwarded to the Commissioner of Lights and the undersigned, and are carefully checked with a view to ascertaining whether the articles asked for are actually required. When the list has been approved, it is returned to the agent with instructions to advertise publicly in the press, calling for tenders for the supplies in question, where it is considered advisable, or to distribute a list of the department's requirements to the leading Arms in their respective lines, in order that they may have an opportunity of quoting. Tenders are received and a tabulated list prepared and forwarded to the purchasing and contract agent at Ottawa with the recommendation of the agent. .Tenders are carefully gone over and the contract awarded in accordance with the prices submitted, that is to say, that the lowest tender is always accepted, quality being equal. As regards purchases made by local agents from time to time to meet the daily requirements of the service, quotations are obtained locally from the respective merchants and the order placed with the firm quoting the lowest price. The agent issues an order known as an emergency order, giving full particulars, prices to be paid, etc., and in order to protect the department against any overcharge, the following is printed across the face of the order:	'This	order is given
and accepted with the distinct understanding that the prices charged are subject to the approval of the purchasing and contract agent of the Department of Marine and Fisheries at Ottawa. This fully protects" the department, even in the event of an agent placing an order at prices which might be considered excessive.
As regards purchases made directly from Ottawa, it is the rule to forward the leading merchants and importers in their respective lines an inquiry with the request to quote and the order is placed with the party quoting the i most advantageous price. This
method is always followed in making purchases.
As regards the repairs to vessels, before any work is placed in hand, the department ship's husband and chief inspector of boilers and machinery make a thorough inspection, prepare specification in detail of the repairs required, which specification is submitted to the leading repair firms in the locality where the repairs are to be effected, with the request that they submit sealed tenders in writing. A careful estimate of the cost- of the repairs is prepared at the same time as the specification. This estimate is forwarded to Ottawa immediately. The tenders are opened by the agent in the presence of another officer, and the result of the tenders forwarded to Ottawa by telegram, and in all cases the lowest tender is accepted, provided that it agrees within reasonable limits of the estimate prepared by the inspector.
The acceptance of the tenders is authorized from Ottawa by wire and is followed by official warrant authorizing the repairs in question, stating the name of the successful tenderer and the amount of his tender, and no work is placed on hand, of any kind whatsoever, until authority is obtained from Ottawa. This system works very satisfactorily. Little or no time is lost, and the department's interests are absolutely safeguarded. In the event of the lowest tender being considerably in excess of the estimate, new tenders, are called for. The tender accepted invariably agrees very closely with the estimated cost prepared by the inspectors, who have a thorough knowledge of the cost of making repairs in the different localities. Speaking generally, at least 90 per cent of the repairs to the vessels are effected at the estimated cost. All supplies are purchased and all repairs to vessels made on a competitive basis whenever and wherever it is possible to do so.

Did the Burrell-Johnson
Company submit tenders for the repairs to the lightship Lurcher?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Probably so; there is scarcely a piece of work we have in that part of the country in Tespect of which we do not receive tenders from the Burrell-Johnson Company.
Who has the purchasing of the small supplies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The emergency supplies
are bought by the agents of the department at the port where they are required.
Who is the agent at Yarmouth?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yarmouth is under the
Halifax agency, which is under the control of Mr. Harvey; the lightship Lurcher is under the control of the agent at St. John. Most of the supplies are got from headquarters, but I presume that if anything were wanted it would be bought by the captain, who would pay for it and send the bill to the agent for approval.

To whom does the captain
at Yarmouth go to for his supplies?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not understand what extra supplies the Lurcher has to purchase. There is a contract with the steward to supply food to the officers and men.

Hundreds of dollars' worth
of supplies are bought there for which tenders are not asked. Here is one item on page N-83 of the Auditor General's Report; E. K. Spinney, $798.46. To whom does the captain apply when he is instructed by the agent at St. John to purchase these goods?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
All goods bought for the
Lurcher lightship, which is connected with the agency at St. John, are bought through that agency, and are purchased on a competitive basis from those firms in Yarmouth which are adjacent to the Lurcher lightship. The prices are subject to the approval of the purchasing and contract agent in Ottawa; I have read to the hon. gentleman the provision in that regard. There is practically nothing, as I understand it, bought by the captain of the Lurcher himself.
It is bought through the agent at the headquarters of that vessel. The headquarters of the Lurcher is St. John.
They are purchased in that way, but through some Conservative in Yarmouth.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No, they are not; they are purchased through the agent at St. John.
To whom does the captain of the lightship Lurcher or any other Government boat coming into Yarmouth, wanting supplies, go ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As I understand, the captains do not make purchases. The supplies are purchased by the agents. The captain would make requisitions and let the agent know what was required, but the purchases are made by the agent, who alone is responsible, although they come to the contracting agent at Ottawa, who examines them to satisfy himself that the prices are proper prices. No one outside of the properly appointed officials of the department has any authority to purchase supplies in Yarmouth.
To whom does the agent at St. John apply at Yarmouth to purchase these goods ? How does he know whom to ask for prices ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I presume that the agent himself or some one under him goes to the respective dealers and gets their prices before purchasing. He certainly has no instructions from us to go to any particular persons. His instructions are to purchase goods at fair, proper and reasonable prices.

I do not think that the agent at St. John deals directly with the firms in Yarmouth. I think the purchases are made through some member of the patronage committee in Yarmouth. The minister knows there is a patronage committee there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I fancy that the only large supplies which are purchased there are in connection with the repairs to ships. In such a case, Mr. MeConlcey, the ship's husband at Ottawa, goes down and arranges for the repairs required at the best possible prices. The agent of the department, purchasing small supplies required at Yarmouth, goes to the different merchants in the town and gets their prices. Of course, he would have a reasonable idea of the value of goods and would know what was a proper price to pay; but even then, his judgment is subject to the approval of the department here, and the goods are sold knowing that the prices charged may not be paid if Mr. Doutre says the prices are too high, but there are no instructions to go to any particular persons.
Then the purchases are not made through any patronage committee in the town of Yarmouth ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.

In running over a comparison of the prices, I see that in one* or two instances the prices in Yarmouth are lower than in other places. For instance, Gillette's lye, which is used in large quantities, is $3.65 a ease in Yarmouth. In St. John, the constituency represented by the minister, it is $3.85; but at Quebec the department pays $4. If the minister wants to purchase his goods cheaply he ought to go to Yarmouth to purchase. At page N-89 I notice a purchase of 300 bushels of oats, middlings and bran, by the department in Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is purchased to take down to Sable island.

I would refer the hon.
member for Peel (Mr. Blain) to N-19, of the Auditor General's Report, where he will find $1,125 spent in repairs to the Lans-downe, which 1 understood was admitted to have been done without any tender or con-

tract. At page N-24 he will find an item paid to Geo. T. Davie & Sons, repairs to the Montcalm, of $4,068.64, without tender or contract. The minister admitted that these repairs were without contract.
Mr. HAZEN. The hon. member will remember that I explained that Davie is the only one below Montreal having a dock in which repairs could be made to the bottom of a vessel. If the repairs were not made there the vessel would have to be taken to the dry dock at Halifax and there would not be much competition there. It might happen that a vessel would be in such a condition that she could not, be taken to Halifax. It does not follow, however, that too much is paid as the work is gone over by Mr. MeConkey, the ship's [DOT]husband, and by the officials of the department and they agree on a price, which in their opinion is fair and reasonable. The case that was referred to in Charlottetown was one in which the firm of Bruce Stewart was the only firm able to handle that class of work.

That is hardly a good
excuse. You might say that if a vessel in Pictou harbour happened to require repairs there "was only one firm in Pictou who could [DOT]make the repairs. But Charlottetown is only 'across the strait and a very short voyage. If the minister is going to act on grounds of that kind he will not resort to tender and contract at all. If repairs amounting to $3,000 or $4,000 are thought not worth offering to tender I am afraid that the principle, is not very well carried out by the present Administration.

The hon. member for Guys-borough is altogether away from the question that was up for discussion between my hon. friend and myself. My hon. friend twitted me for not standing by the same principles that I advocated on the other side of the House. Will my hon. friend tell me when I ever suggested during the time I was on the other side of the House that small repairs should be let by public tender? Everybody knows that it would not be possible for any Government to ask for tenders for repairs to vessels or docks, as specifications could not be written for them, and without a specification you could not receive tenders; or the tenders would be of no value. What I said on the other side of the House was that contracts to supply goods in large quantities should be let by public competition. I answer my hon. friend by saying that the Government- of which I am now a supporter has been doing that ever since they came into office in 1911. When my hon. friend tries to sidetrack the issue by pointing out from the Auditor General's Report that this Government allowed repairs to be made to vessels without competition, he is not meeting the case at all.
Does the hon. gentleman say that this Government has given out no new work for the building of wharfs without tender and contract?

I speak subject to correction, but I do not think this Government has given out contracts where the amount is more than $5,000 as provided by statute without first asking for tenders. Can my bon. friend give me a case?
I have three in my county.
How much do they amount to?
I am not talking about the amount.
It makes all the difference.

My hon. friend from
Guysborough was saying that the hon. member for Peel is not taking the same stand as he did in previous years. I can name three wharfs constructed on the Mira river last year without tender and contract.
All new wharfs?
Yes.
Amounting to how much in each case?

I am not in'a position
to say.
The principle is the same.

The principle is not the
same.

I could give my hon. friend another case where breastworks were built on the Lingan Bar without tenders and contract. I take the ground that everything, even to the amount of $500 should be given out by tender and contract, and if the late Government did not do that with new wharfs, they were making a serious mistake.
Would my hon. friend limit it to $500?
I would not limit it at all.	.

My hon. friend is laying down a new policy for his party; because the hon. gentlemen around him listened to the ministers of their party, declaring time and time again from their places in this House when in office that where a tender did not exceed $5,000, as provided by statute, it was understood and agreed between the two parties-
No, no.
I could turn up ' Hansard,' and show where my hon. friend from Carle-ton defended his Government in doing that.
Turn it up.
You will deny it as you did with the Postmaster General.

I will deal with my hon. friend from Lincoln later, but I tell my hon. friend from Peel that he cannot find anything like that on ' Hansard.' I might have said the Government have the right in an emergency-
No, not in an emergency.

Yes, to let a contract
not exceeding $5,000 without tender, but if the hon. member can find that I ever voiced the sentiment that it was a proper thing for this Government to let contracts for $5,000 without tender, I will apologize. It is a question of policy, not of what the law allows. If the Government were allowed to carry out the policy the hon. member has enunciated here to-day it would practically eliminate the question of tender and contract in matters amounting to millions of dollars, because every year millioas are expended under $5,000. My hon. friend can see the difference. The law gives the Government the right to enter into contract without tender if the amount does not exceed $5,000.
My understanding is-I speak subject to correction from the Minister of Marine and Fisheries-that this regulation about the $5,000 applies only to the Department of Public Works.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As my hon. friend has referred to me, my understanding is that it applies to all public works whether under the direction of the Public Works Department or any other department of Government. It was decided that printing was a public work under the statute.

I thought it referred to the Public Works Department only. I never heard it applied to ships in the Marine Department. My hon. friend from Peel is not so familiar with the question of repairs to ships as I am. It is a matter on which I can speak with some authority because I know how the business is done. If he goes to any of the large shipyards in England he will constantly find the parties who bring their ships into the dock for repairs, asking for tenders from all who do that class of work. The fact that it is repairs, does not preclude the asking for tenders in any sense. There is no difficulty at all in that. There might be difficulty where a boiler had to be taken out when its condition was unknown. It is easy to see what repairs are required and to ask for tenders. My hon. friend is mistaken when he says that repairs cannot be subject to tender and contract like any other work. I never heard my hon. friend take the stand that the amount must be over $5,000. It is the first time I ever heard him make that statement in the House.

Did my hon. friend ever
hear his own Government make that statement?

We all recollect what
the hon. member stood for, and I am in the kindliest way requesting him to try and impress the views he held on this side of the House for ten years on the Government he now supports, and insist that they carry out those principles.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I would like to say to my hon. friend from Guysborough that tenders were asked for repair work amounting to $1,100, that Mr. Heims was the lowest tenderer and that the work was done by contract. Some repair work can be done by contract and some cannot. We have to be guided by the ship's husband as to whether it can or not.
Construction of lighthouses, including the regulation of traffic in the Detroit river and such other places as may be found necessary, $1,000,000.

As I understand, the Government has undertaken to establish [DOT] a harbour at Port Nelson. A beginning of expenditure in establishing a harbour at that port has been made. I am not aware which particular department is going to be responsible for these improvements. Ordinarily, I presume that it would be the Department of Public Works, but in the discussion of the Railway Estimates it appeared that the Railway Department was

12n7
taking up the question and had made the expenditure that had been made up to that time. But it was also made apparent that the Department of Marine and Fisheries had undertaken a certain responsibility in regard to this harbour with reference to surveys and safeguarding. I would like to know which department is going to be responsible for developing this port.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The work of providing the terminals, and other work that is necessary at Port Nelson, is being done by the Department of Railways and Canals as the terminal work is work of a character which is necessary in order to enable the Hudson Bay railway, that is being built by the Department of Railways and Canals, to ship freight through that port. With the work of providing wharfs, dredging the channel and providing the terminal facilities that are necessary my department has nothing to do. The Department of Marine and Fisheries will be charged with the responsibility of providing the necessary aids to navigation, such as buoys and lighthouses. The Naval Department, which is under the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and which has charge of the wireless telegraphy, will also have to, as a part of the aids to navigation, establish certain wireless telegraph stations along that route. The 'question is one that has been giving the members of the lighthouse board a great deal of concern. The lighthouses of this country are in a sense controlled by the lighthouse board which consists of the deputy minister, the inspector of lights, the chief engineer of the department, and a number of gentlemen who are not officials of the department, like the President of the Dominion Marine Association and of the Shipping Federation of Canada and, I think, some other gentle-Vnen from the Pacific coast. All questions about the establishment of new lights are submitted to the board. They recommend to the minister where new lights should be established, whether new lights should be improved, where new buoys should be placed and where submarine bells should be stationed. The question of aids to navigation has been carefully considered by the board and I might state what has been done up to the present time and what the board decided to do at a meeting held in the city of Ottawa within, the last few days. The record in the department indicates that in the early part of September, 1912, the department received a suggestion from Mr. Clergue of the Hudson Bay Steam-77J
boat Company that certain marks be placed at the mouth of the Nelson river. The deputy minister and the chief engineer and the commissioner of lights held a consultation on the matter and decided to forward that fall aboard the ' Beothic ' fifteen small buoys (unlighted) complete with moorings. When this decision was taken it was expected that the Beothic would come to Montreal and accordingly arrangements were made to furnish 15 buoys from that agency. Two or three days lateT uncertainty arose as to whether or not the Beothic would come to Montreal and arrangements were accordingly made to forward 15 buoys from Halifax via Sydney. The Beothic afterwards came to Quebec and as two sets of buoys had been prepared and as it was believed that the entire 30 would ultimately be needed in the neighbourhood of Nelson, they were forwarded aboard the Beothic.
It developed, however, that on the arrival of the Beothic at Nelson in the fall of 1912 there were no facilities for landing 15 of the heavier buoys and the 30 moorings. Two of the heavier buoys were left in position at the mouth of the Nelson river by the captain of the Beothic; 13 heavier buoys and the 30 moorings were fetched back to Halifax, while 15 of the lighter buoys with wire moorings but without anchors were landed at Churchill and placed in care of the Mounted Police. At the lighthouse board meeting, February 6, 1913, consideration was given to a report prepared by Mr. F. Anderson of the Hydrographic Survey having reference to the needs in the way of aids to navigation in northern waters. Decision was deferred and the matter was referred to the chief engineer and the commissioner of lights to be further considered in consultation with Mr. Anderson. On March 14, the chief engineer and the commissioner of lights discussed the matter with Mr. Anderson and with Mr. Hazen, resident engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals for Hudson bay, and decided to provide 16 steel buoys, 4 of them to carry top marks and also 12 spar buoys. It was hoped that arrangements could be made with the Department of Railways and Canals for placing the buoys m position and maintaining them. It was intended to for-, ward them to Hudson bay in the summer of 1913, but unfortunately occasion for so doing did not present itself. When in the latter part of June there seemed to be no opportunity to forward this material, the commissioner of lights discussed the matter with the chief hydrographer. It appeared that the Beothic was being chartered

by the Department of Naval Service and that should it be necessary for that department to fit her up as a survey steamer, there would be no available space for the accommodation of buoys and moorings, also that the Minto, should she proceed to Hudson bay, might not probably be ready to sail before the 1st August, 1913. It seemed to the commissioner of lights scarcely worth while sending the buoys aboard the Minto and placing them for the few weeks of navigation that might remain, but it was suggested that if the Minto sailed in that direction the buoys might be forwarded and stored at some convenient point ready for placing in the spring of 1914. Doubt was expressed as to whether any person outside of the Hydrographic Survey would have sufficient local knowledge to place the buoys. As it turned out the Minto did not go to Hudson bay during the season of 1913. Further consideration was given to the matter of aids to navigation by the lighthouse board on the 2nd July, 1913, and in view of the circumstances of the case including the difficulty of transportation or supplies, the board deferred action until next year, pending a further report from the Hydrographic Survey. This further report was received on the 6th instant and is listed for consideration at the next meeting of the lighthouse board. This matter was taken up later on by the board and they have decided on a certain course of action during the coming summer. They are organizing for it now. They have had as thorough reports as they could get about the straits and they have decided to place -twelve lighthouses in the straits commencing at the entrance and running up to Port Nelson. Further information will be obtained during the coming season; a boat will probably be sent up there with a party on board to make observations as to where these lighthouses should be placed. The lighthouse board will fix the location of these twelve lighthouses and others will also have to be placed. When the Naval Estimates come before the House there will be found in the vote for wireless telegraph an appropriation to establish a wireless station somewhere along the straits.
Those who have traversed these waters are of opinion that the wireless will be of the greatest possible aid to navigation, because the wireless operater in clear weather from the height of land along the shore, can with powerful glasses observe the movement of the ice in the Straits and convey the information by wireless to ships coming

through, so as to enable them to pursue the safest course. Of course, in those waters, which freeze over in winter, the buoys have to be removed before the ice forms and replaced after it disappears, and there will he difficulties encountered, but I have no doubt these difficulties will he overcome as we get further information on the subject. It is our intention to get in operation this year twelve lighthouses and the wireless station, and to acquire further information as to what may be necessary for the future.

The Quebec Government is subsidizing a railway to be constructed in the direction of James bay, and it is of great interest to us that the possibility of a safe harbour in James bay should be ascertained. Has anything been done with regard to that? I understand the first expedition has been sent and soundings have been taken, and a programme laid out for the future. Will there be further exploration?	.
* Mr. HAZEN: The only thing my department is charged with in that regard is as to the furnishing of aids to navigation. We have nothing to do with selecting a harbour at James bay. I presume my hon. friend refers to the idea that a great deal of the grain that would come to Port Nelson might be brought to James bay and thence by rail to Quebec. That matter would be in the Railway Department. A steamer, under the command of Captain Anderson, has been in the Hudson bay for the last two years, doing hydrographic work, but I do not think anything has been done with reference to the location of a harbour in James bay.

The province of Quebec has great hope from this James Bay railway, and indeed it will be found to be not only a provincial, hut, eventually, a national enterprise. The minister knows the possibilities of that railway, if ever it is constructed, and I believe that every reasonable expenditure, to locate the most available harbour in James hay, would be Teadily sanctioned bjv this side of the House. I understand that Mr. Clergue has practically located his line. Speaking for those who come from Quebec, and who are more intimately in touch with the ' provincial authorities, and who expect a great deal from that enterprise, I can assure the minister that anything the department can do towards locating a terminus, and equipping it for the James Bay

railway, will be heartily endorsed by this side of the House.

What we are particularly concerned in knowing is what share of responsibility for the disasters, which occurred to the vessels sent up to Hudson bay, should the Marine Department assume. The record appears to have been very bad. Three of the vessels, which amounted to anything, did not get there, although the three smaller vessels did, and when the matter was under discussion before, the idea was given out by the Railway Department that the trouble occurred because of the fault of the Marine Department in not having provided aids to navigation. Damage has been done to the welfare of this country because of the disasters that overtook the steamers that went to the Hudson bay last summer, and whether the blame belongs to the Marine Department or to the Railway Department, we want to have it placed on the proper shoulders. What I am anxious about is, that the natural conditions shall not be blamed for failures which have occurred, because of some lack in the administration of one department or the other. The Railway Department has blamed the Marine Department, and now I want to know from the Marine Department exactly what was done, and if the department considers that what was done by it was sufficient to have protected the vessels which met with disaster.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Of course, we have no
organization in that district; we have no agencies, or employees, or anything of that sort We were given to understand by Mr. Clergue, who seems greatly interested, that if we furnish these buoys they would be placed, through the instrumentality of these gentlemen who were then there. It was with that understanding that the Marine Department sent these buoys up to Port Nelson.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Yes, but they would be for the season of 1913. As I pointed out, difficulties occurred about getting the buoys placed and in landing of them. I understood that thirty buoys should have left there, but only fifteen were left and the others sent on later when they could be of no use in the season 1913. But we did what we were asked to do, that is to send the buoys, but as to whether the accidents that occurred were the fault of the Railways' Department or the Marine Department is
open to question. I did not understand the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) to attempt to throw blame on the Marine Department, but gathered from his discussion of the matter that he thought the blame was due to defective orders on the part of the captains of these boats. But, as I have said, the Department was asked to send these buoys, and the buoys were sent with the understanding that they were to be placed by others. We had no boats going uip, nor any available to go. With the work mapped out by the Lighthouse Board, we hope that great improvement will take place in the navigation of the Straits. Nelson harbour, as hon. gentlemen know, will require a great deal of dredging, as the water is shallow, and very extensive harbour work. Until the dredging and harbour works are completed there will be more or less difficulty with vessels going there getting safe landing or safe anchorage. B: t when the works are finished, as I understand from the reports of engineers who have been there, there will be a very good harbour, one where vessels will be safe.

Did not the Marine
Department have a vessel there last summer?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No the only vessel on Hudson bay that we had anything to do with was the hydrographic survey vessel which has been there for two seasons under command of Captain Anderson, an old official of the Department who is taking soundings and carrying on the other work of the hydrographic survey.

What is her name? I
understood it was the Acadia.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I thought it was a different vessel, but the Deputy Minister tells me it was the Acadia.

In the discussion in the
House, it was assumed that the Acadia was there. But that is not the point. It seems to me that a very remarkable condition has been disclosed. I do not know whether one department of the Government operates without regard to the other; but it must have been known by the departments of the Government generally that there was to be a serious undertaking by the Railway Department during last summer looking to the 'beginning of the development of this port. My hon. friend has said that there are natural difficulties there. That being so, it was to be expected that the Marine Department would provide aids to naviga-

tion to enable the Department of Railways to properly carry on its work. I think it is a somewhat remarkable method of handling business that my hon. friend has shown. A number of buoys or guides to navigation were sent up, but with no arrangement for placing them so that they might really be of assistance to navigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Rut the difficulty was that nobody had knowledge as to where to place them, and until we could get a report from the Hydrographic Survey last year that knowledge could not be had. No survey had been made before with a view to ascertaining that.

I am not questioning that. But when the Railway Estimates were up it was pointed out that there must have been lack of foresight, for it appeared that shipments were made there without due preparation for their proper landing and for the safety of the ships. It matters not whether the Department of Marine had arrangements made beforehand or not. The point is that the Government undertook to do some things they were not prepared to do, and they suffered disaster because of [DOT] unpreparedness. That is a very important consideration,- and one that I think the country should be thoroughly aware of- that the Government undertook certain work at Port Nelson without having made proper preparations for it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But ships have been going through the straits to Port Nelson for years.

But these ships of the Government sent during 1913 did hot get to Port Nelson, land their cargoes and return in safety. With the whole of the resources of this country at the disposal of this Government, with a Hydrographic Survey in operation, with a Department of Marine in operation-a department that shipped out an ample number of guides to navigation to a port such as this, but without any arrangement for placing those guides-I think this a most deplorable exposure of lack of proper attention to the work in hand, or lack of appreciation of the importance of the work and the importance of its being done without mishap in order that an unfortunate impression might not be created as to the success of the route when established.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We had no lack of appreciation of the difficulty when we sent the buoys up there, and we had every

reason to believe from the conversations we had with the engineer in charge and with Mr. Clergue that these buoys would be properly placed.
By whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: By the gentlemen who were there. But, as I told the committee, the difficulty was to get the buoys landed when they got there. 1 Mr. Clergue came to me about it and was deeply interested. I took it from what he told me that these buoys would be placed; all he asked was to let him have them. But it is a long distance away, and such difficulties arose as occur in every work of that sort, and so the buoys did not get placed. But I feel that the officers of the Department of Marine were not to blame for that. It was simply one of those things which occur that are not foreseen. I fail to see what more could be done. We had no organization there, and we sent the buoys under the belief-and having reason for that belief-that they would be properly placed. I do not think there is anything to show that the fact that they are not properly placed was not because of accident.

There is no question that the accidents occurred, and no question, that the intention in sending the buoys was to prevent accident. There is no question that the buoys were not properly placed, and from what I can learn from the minister he had no reason to believe that the buoys would be property placed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have told the hon. gentleman that I had very reasonable grounds which were based upon the conversations I and my departmental officers had with Mr. Clergue and with officials who were up there, as was stated in the memorandum I read to my hon. friend.
What is the responsibility of Mr. Clergue in the matter; is he a private citizen or a Government official?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

speechtext:
It is quite evident that
for one reason or other the work of the development of Port Nelson will be very much minimized during the coming summer, if not prevented altogether, by reason of the disasters of last summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do .not think that is a
logical deduction.

My hon. friend sends up to Port Nelson a vessel of 1,790 tons, which is wrecked and the cargo lost, and another vessel of 2,020 tons, which brings its cargo back. He sends another vessel of 1,937 tons, which does not land its cargo. Three vessels of 500 tons or less are the only ones of the whole expedition that land their cargoes; two of them, however, made a second trip. Roughly speaking, there were 2,500 tons landed at Nelson and something like 4,000 or 5,000 tons that were not landed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That has nothing to do
with aids to navigation. The failure to land those cargoes was not due to the absence of lighthouses or things of that
sort; it was because of the lack of terminal facilities at the port.

Let it be the fault of one department or of the other, the result is that out of a total requirement, according to the Government's own estimate, of some
7,000	tons of material, only 2,500 tons were landed, and because of that the development of the port during the coming summer must necessarily be practically at a standstill. That is a deplorable condition, and whether it is the fault of the Railway department or of the Marine department, it is certainly the fault of the Government, and the Government will have to shoulder the blame.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think it is the
fault of either department; it is because of natural conditions which could not be overcome in that time. Of course the Opposition's business is to assume that the Government is to blame.

When a government undertaking such a great work as the development of Port Nelson starts in this way, it is a very poor indication of the success that is going to be achieved, and that is the way it will be looked at by the public at large. The route as a transportation proposition is discredited by reason or the failure of the Government during the past summer.
I think my hon. friend and his colleagues do not appreciate the position in its full importance, and I am trying to impress it upon them very strongly. The suggestion that the hon. minister has taken proper means to take care of the channel at Port Nelson as it exists to-day by landing buoys at Churchill or bringing them back to Halifax is something that is supremely ridiculous.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The captains of the vessels said it could not be helped.

I am willing to accept the position as my hon. friend has stated it; I think he has placed his department and the Government in the worst light he possibly could. The question I want to ask the minister is this: has the Government through the medium of his or any other department, arrived at a conclusion as to what amount of work will be necessary at Port Nelson to make it a practicable port, what will be the cost of that work, and how long it will take to complete it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
All my department has to do with is aids to navigation. The survey, which is practically completed, is of

far more importance than anything else so far as safety of navigation is concerned. With -that survey made, and the information now available for the first time, we are in a position to go ahead with intelligence and place these aids to navigation, and we are making arrangements to do it as soon as possible. So far as the cost of the development of the port is concerned, meaning, I presume, the providing of port facilities in the way of docks, elevators, dredging and other harbour *works, I am unable to give my hon. friend an answer, as. this does not fall within my department. I think he will have to repeat that question to the Minister of Railways when his Estimates are before the House, or on some other occasion.

Can the minister say if the Government has arrived at any knowledge as to what the extent of the dredging operations required will be? That surely must be arrived at as a result of the investigations conducted by my hon. friend's department.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is not under my department at all; my department has nothing to do with dredging, as I have explained. Any investigation into the quantity of dredging that will be required or into the cost of these harbour works would be a matter for the Department of Railways and Canals.

I pressed the question because I understood the Hydrographic Survey was acting at Port Nelson and, in my innocence, assumed that the purpose of the survey was to give the Government accurate information as to what the requirements would be. I am not aware that the Railway Department are pursuing any investigations of that nature and so I am bound to assume that the Government have decided to create a new port without knowledge as to what the expense will be or what work will be required or how long it will take.
I think it is a most deplorable condition.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend has no right to assume from anything that has occurred to-night that what he says is the case. I think he will find that the Railway Department, which has had its engineers up there for some time, will have full reports Showing exactly what is required.
I shall be glad to take the matter up with the Minister of Railways, but it is an important question and I have no apology to offer for pressing the point.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I would be the last man to suggest that the hon. member should offer an apology. He has done nothing outside the bounds of fair parliamentary criticism.

I would remind the
minister of an order of the House in response to a motion which I placed on the first. Order Paper of the session, asking for tenders and contracts for work at Grande Anse. The papers have not yet been brought down.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall see that the return is brought down at once. The amount of the contract was $1,100, and it was awarded to Geo. Eddy of Bathurst.
Could the minister give any information about a new signal station at White Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am informed that that
work has been completed, I think it is at Whitehead island. It is a fog alarm building. The' contract price was $6,850, and the work is completed and should be in operation by this time.
Telephones in connection with aids to navigation, $5,000.
How will this $5,000 be distributed?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
A small amount is being
expended each year in bringing some of the more important outlying stations into telephonic communication with the nearest settlements. This is useful for sending meteorological reports and in case of accident or shipwreck. Last year we spent only $738.15 of this amount. That was to connect Leonard Island, B.C., with Tofino telegraph office.
I see nothing in this for Gloucester county?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That service is in connection with the life-saving station, and is provided for in connection with the service to which it belongs.
Pensions to retired pilots, $5,700.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It has always been customary to add the names of pilots to whom these pensions are paid, and I would like the item to be amended, giving the names of the pilots.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Amendment agreed to.
I see there is a decrease of $600? Does that mean that two pilots have died?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
It means two pilots less; they get $300 each.
To replace Scout, $9,000.
Where is the Scout?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Scout has gone up.
We have a new vessel being built by the Poison Iron Works, Limited, Toronto, contract price $173,399.
To replace Maisonneuve, $40,000.
Was a contract let for this work?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No, we are going to build it at the Government shipyard at Sorel.
Allowance to Harbour Master, Amherstburg, $400.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My hon. friend will find
that in almost every year. At Amherst-burg we have to do a lot of supervision of lights and buoys in the Detroit river and lake Erie. We have no agency there so we pay the Harbour Master $400 for doing the work, which is most economical for the department.
Meteorological Service, $213,000.

Were the instruments
purchased in the United States?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not think so.
What is the large increase for?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The increase asked for is
to cover additional expenses in connection with the printing of two and possibly three annual meteorological reports; there is an increase in the appropriation for instruments, a residence is provided for the director and a well deserved increase in the salaries of the officers of the staff. They were very low before.
Marine hospitals, $75,000.
Does that mean an increase in the number of hospitals or an increase in the cost of operating those now in existence?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
An increase in the cost of operating those now in existence. My hon. friend knows that practically all the marine hospitals have been abolished. For instance in the city of St. John there used to be a very fine marine hospital which is now used as a home for incurables. There was another one at Pictou, but some years ago the policy was adopted of closing up these hospitals in towns where there were
public hospitals and arrangements were made with the trustees of the public hospitals at a per diem allowance, which costs the department less and the sailors get much better treatment.

I think we should have a marine hospital at Canso, as a great many fishermen call there and a great deal of hardship is endured for want of a marine hospital. I brought this matter to the minister's attention the last two sessions, and I would like to know if he has arrived at a conclusion in the matter ?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is there no public hospital in Canso ?

No, nor anywhere near Canso, Louisburg is the nearest, and that is a long distance away. As Canso is a place of call for a great many vessels not only belonging to the port but also from Lunenburg and other parts of Nova Scotia, this is a question of very great importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that to establish new marine hospitals is entirely contrary to the policy the department has been pursuing for the last 15 years. The policy of abolishing these hospitals commenced when Sir Hibbert Tupper was Minister of Marine, and has been followed by all his successors in that department. How large a town is Canso ?
About 1,700 people by the census.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In the small towns in my province, such as Bathurst, Chatham, Moncton, St. John, Fredericton and St. Stephen, the hospitals are aided by a provincial grant and also by the town; then there are private benefactions. Perhaps in Canso there will be a hospital of that sort established soon. I should think the cost would be very considerable, and I doubt if the circumstances of the case-I speak subject to correction-would justify the outlay. I would suggest that perhaps it would be a good thing for my hon. friend to get some of the public-spirited citizens of the town to take the matter up and if they once established the hospital I am sure they would never be without it again.

I thought I could appeal to my hon. friend, as Canso is the headquarters of the fishing industry of eastern Nova Scotia and a shelter for the fleet operating on the Grand Banks. I have seen the harbour crowded with these fishing vessels and something like 300 sailors in the town at one time. As my hon. friend

[DOT]does not seem to be making any progress in the question of free medicine, I thought he might regard this as an opportunity for doing something material for the fishermen of Nova Scotia.
I would like to ask the minister if he will permit any reconsideration or discussion of any of these items?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Certainly, in discussing these items we have not tied ourselves down to the particular item under consideration. If there is any further information that the hon. gentleman wants about any item I shall be very glad to give it to him, no matter what the item is that is under consideration.
Progress reported.	.
On- motion of Mr. Hazen, the House adjourned' at 11.30 p.m.
Monday, March 2, 1914.
